\textbf{Theorem 88} (Moments from the log partition function). \emph{For
an exponential family \[p(y;\eta)=h(y)\exp(\eta^T T(y)-A(\eta)),\] we
have \[\nabla_\eta A(\eta)=\mathbb{E}_\eta[T(Y)]\] and
\[\nabla_\eta^2 A(\eta)=\operatorname{Cov}_\eta(T(Y)).\] In the
one-dimensional case, \[A'(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[T(Y)],
\qquad
A''(\eta)=\operatorname{Var}(T(Y)).\]}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

In one dimension, \[A(\eta)=\log\int h(y)e^{\eta T(y)}\,dy.\]
Differentiate:
\[A'(\eta)=\frac{\int T(y)h(y)e^{\eta T(y)}\,dy}{\int h(y)e^{\eta T(y)}\,dy}.\]
Since \[p(y;\eta)=h(y)e^{\eta T(y)-A(\eta)},\] the derivative becomes
\[A'(\eta)=\int T(y)p(y;\eta)\,dy=\mathbb{E}[T(Y)].\] Differentiating
again gives
\[A''(\eta)=\mathbb{E}[T(Y)^2]-(\mathbb{E}[T(Y)])^2=\operatorname{Var}(T(Y)).\]
The multidimensional version replaces derivatives by gradients and
Hessians.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example 89} (Bernoulli moments from \(A(\eta)\)). For Bernoulli
in canonical form, \[A(\eta)=\log(1+e^\eta).\] Use derivatives of \(A\)
to find \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

First, \[A'(\eta)=\frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}=\mu.\]
Therefore \[\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mu.\] Second,
\[A''(\eta)=\frac{e^\eta}{(1+e^\eta)^2}=\mu(1-\mu).\] Thus
\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mu(1-\mu).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Location and Scale Families}\label{location-and-scale-families}

This section introduces another unifying idea: many distributions are
obtained by shifting and rescaling a standard distribution.

\subsection{Definition}\label{definition-1}

This subsection defines the location-scale family through a
transformation of a standard random variable.

\textbf{Definition 90} (Location-scale family). Let \(X\) be a random
variable with CDF \(F\) and pdf \(f\). For constants
\(\mu\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\sigma>0\), define \[Y=\mu+\sigma X.\] Then
\(Y\) belongs to the location-scale family generated by \(X\). Its pdf
is \[f_Y(y)=\frac1\sigma f\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right).\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The formula follows from the change of variables
\[x=\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma},
\qquad
\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac1\sigma.\] Therefore
\[f_Y(y)=f_X\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\left|\frac1\sigma\right|.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Examples of location-scale
families}\label{examples-of-location-scale-families}

This subsection lists familiar distributions that fit the location-scale
framework.

Examples include:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  normal distribution;
\item
  Cauchy distribution;
\item
  continuous uniform distribution;
\item
  discrete uniform distribution in certain shifted/scaled forms;
\item
  logistic distribution;
\item
  Laplace distribution;
\item
  Student's \(t\) distribution.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Example 91} (Normal location-scale transformation). If
\(Z\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,1)\) and \(Y=\mu+\sigma Z\), find the
distribution of \(Y\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The standard normal density is \[f_Z(z)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}.\]
Using the location-scale formula,
\[f_Y(y)=\frac1\sigma \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\right]
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\left[-\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right].\]
Thus \[Y\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem 92} (Uniform location-scale transformation).
Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and \(Y=a+(b-a)X\) where
\(a<b\). Find the distribution of \(Y\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here \(\mu=a\) and \(\sigma=b-a\). Since \(X\) is uniform on \([0,1]\),
the transformation maps \([0,1]\) to \([a,b]\). The density is
\[f_Y(y)=\frac1{b-a},
\qquad a\le y\le b.\] Therefore \[Y\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Additional Practice
Problems}\label{additional-practice-problems}

This section provides extra problems with solutions to reinforce the
core skills of Section 2.

\textbf{Practice Problem 93} (Classify random variables). Classify each
random variable as discrete, continuous, or mixed.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Number of emails received in one hour.
\item
  Time until the next email arrives.
\item
  A variable that equals \(0\) with probability \(0.3\) and otherwise is
  uniform on \([1,2]\).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

(a) The number of emails is a count, so it is discrete. A Poisson model
may be appropriate.

(b) Waiting time is measured on a continuum, so it is continuous. An
exponential model may be appropriate.

(c) This variable has a point mass at \(0\) and a continuous component
on \([1,2]\), so it is mixed.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem 94} (From density to probability). Let \[f(x)=
\begin{cases}
cx, & 0\le x\le 2,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] Find \(c\) and compute \(\mathbb{P}(1\le X\le 2)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The total area must be \(1\):
\[1=\int_0^2 cx\,dx=c\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^2=2c.\] Thus
\(c=1/2\). Then
\[\mathbb{P}(1\le X\le 2)=\int_1^2 \frac{x}{2}\,dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^2=1-\frac14=\frac34.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem 95} (Choosing the right distribution). For each
story, choose a reasonable distribution.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Count the number of defective items in \(20\) independent items, each
  defective with probability \(0.02\).
\item
  Count the number of arrivals in one minute when arrivals occur at
  average rate \(3\) per minute.
\item
  Time until the first arrival when arrivals occur at average rate \(3\)
  per minute.
\item
  Draw \(5\) cards from a deck without replacement and count the number
  of aces.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

(a) Binomial: \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,0.02)\).

(b) Poisson: \(X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(3)\).

(c) Exponential: \(X\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(3)\).

(d) Hypergeometric: \(N=52\), \(M=4\) aces, \(K=5\) draws, so
\[\mathbb{P}(X=x)=\frac{\binom4x\binom{48}{5-x}}{\binom{52}{5}}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem 96} (Exponential family calculation). Let
\(Y\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\) and use the natural parameter
\(\eta=\log\lambda\). Verify that \(A'(\eta)=\lambda\) and
\(A''(\eta)=\lambda\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For the Poisson exponential family, \[A(\eta)=e^\eta.\] Therefore
\[A'(\eta)=e^\eta=\lambda,\] and \[A''(\eta)=e^\eta=\lambda.\] Since
\(T(Y)=Y\), this agrees with \[\mathbb{E}[Y]=\lambda,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\lambda.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Chapter 3: Joint and Conditional
Probability}\label{chapter-3-joint-and-conditional-probability}

This chapter moves from one random variable to several random variables
studied together. The main objects are joint distributions, marginal
distributions, conditional distributions, independence, covariance,
total probability, Bayes theorem, and conditional independence.

\textbf{Topics.} Expected value review; variance and covariance; joint,
marginal, and conditional distributions; independence; total
probability; Bayes theorem; conditional independence.

\section{Overview}\label{overview}

This section moves from one random variable to several random variables
studied together.

In Section 2, we learned how a single random variable is described by a
CDF, a pmf, or a pdf. In applications, however, data usually come in
groups: height and weight, treatment and outcome, first die and second
die, test result and disease status, or multiple measurements from the
same experiment. The correct mathematical language for this is the
\emph{joint distribution}. Once we have a joint distribution, we can
recover marginal distributions, define conditional distributions, test
independence, and update probabilities using Bayes theorem.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Main message}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A joint distribution describes the complete probabilistic relationship
among variables. Marginal distributions describe individual variables.
Conditional distributions describe what remains after partial
information is known.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Expected Values: Review}\label{expected-values-review}

This section reviews expected value and variance because they are the
basic numerical summaries used throughout joint and conditional
probability.

\subsection{Expected value}\label{expected-value}

This subsection recalls the definition and interpretation of expected
value for discrete and continuous random variables.

\textbf{Definition (Expected value).}

Let \(X\) be a random variable. If \(X\) is discrete with pmf
\(p_X(k)\), then {[} \mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=\sum\emph{\{\text{all }k\} k
p\_X(k). {]} If \(X\) is continuous with pdf \(f_X(x)\), then {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=\int}\{-\infty\}\^{}\{\infty\} x f\_X(x),d x. {]}

Expected value is a generalization of the idea of an average.
Operationally, if we measure \(X\) in many independent trials and obtain
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), then the sample average {[}
\overline X\_n=\frac{1}{n}(X\_1+\cdots+X\_n) {]} should approach
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\) as \(n\) becomes large. This is formalized later by
the Law of Large Numbers.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Proposition: Linearity for one random variable}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For constants \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}aX+b{]}=a\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}+b. {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Bernoulli expected value).}

Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), so {[}
\mathbb{P}(X=0)=1-p,\qquad \mathbb{P}(X=1)=p. {]} Find
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Using the discrete expectation formula, {[} \mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=\sum\_k k
p\_X(k)=0(1-p)+1(p)=p. {]} Thus the expected value of a Bernoulli random
variable is its success probability: {[} \boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=p.} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Expected outcome of a fair die).}

Let \(X\) be the outcome of rolling a fair six-sided die. Find
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The pmf is \(p_X(k)=1/6\) for \(k=1,2,3,4,5,6\). Therefore {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=\sum\_\{k=1\}\^{}\{6\} k\frac{1}{6}
=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6} =\frac{21}{6}=\frac{7}{2}. {]} So the long-run
average die value is {[} \boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=3.5.} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Variance and standard
deviation}\label{variance-and-standard-deviation}

This subsection reviews how variance and standard deviation measure the
spread of a random variable around its mean.

\textbf{Definition (Variance and standard deviation).}

The variance of a random variable \(X\) is {[}
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])\^{}2\right{]}.
{]} The standard deviation is {[}
\operatorname{STD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}. {]}

A useful computational formula is {[}
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}{[}X\^{}2{]}-\left(\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}\right)\^{}2.
{]} For constants \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), {[}
\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a\^{}2\operatorname{Var}(X). {]} Adding a
constant changes location but not spread; multiplying by \(a\) scales
spread by \(a^2\) in variance and by \(|a|\) in standard deviation.

\textbf{Example (Variance of a Bernoulli random variable).}

Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\). Find
\(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(X\) only takes values \(0\) and \(1\), we have \(X^2=X\). Thus
{[} \mathbb{E}{[}X\^{}2{]}=\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=p. {]} Using the
computational formula, {[}
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}{[}X\^{}2{]}-(\mathbb{E}{[}X{]})\textsuperscript{2=p-p}2=p(1-p).
{]} Therefore {[} \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p).} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem (Review: expectation and variance).}

Suppose \(X\) takes values \(-1,0,2\) with probabilities
\(1/4,1/2,1/4\), respectively. Find \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) and
\(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

First compute the mean: {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=(-1)\frac14+0\frac12+2\frac14=-\frac14+\frac12=\frac14.
{]} Next compute the second moment: {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}X\^{}2{]}=(-1)\textsuperscript{2\frac14+0}2\frac12+2\^{}2\frac14=\frac14+1=\frac54.
{]} Therefore {[}
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}{[}X\^{}2{]}-(\mathbb{E}{[}X{]})\textsuperscript{2=\frac54-\left(\frac14\right)}2
=\frac{20}{16}-\frac{1}{16}=\frac{19}{16}. {]} So {[}
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac14,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{19}{16}.}
{]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Joint Distributions}\label{joint-distributions}

This section introduces the joint distribution, which is the main object
for studying two or more random variables together.

\subsection{Joint CDF, joint pmf, and joint
pdf}\label{joint-cdf-joint-pmf-and-joint-pdf}

This subsection defines the joint distribution for two random variables
in both discrete and continuous cases.

\textbf{Definition (Joint CDF).}

For two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the joint cumulative
distribution function is {[} F\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X\le x,,Y\le y).
{]}

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are both discrete, then their joint pmf is {[}
p\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y), {]} for all
\(x\in\mathbb{R}ange(X)\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}ange(Y)\). It must satisfy
{[} p\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)\ge 0, \qquad
\sum\emph{\{x\}\sum}\{y\}p\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=1. {]}

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are absolutely continuous, then their joint pdf
\(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) satisfies {[} f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)\ge 0, \qquad
\int\emph{\{-\infty\}\textsuperscript{\{\infty\}\int\_\{-\infty\}}\{\infty\}f}\{X,Y\}(x,y),d
x,d y=1. {]} When the joint CDF is differentiable, {[}
f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\partial y}F\_\{X,Y\}(x,y).
{]} For a region \(R\) in the \(xy\)-plane, {[}
\mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in R)=\iint\emph{R f}\{X,Y\}(x,y),d x,d y. {]}

\subsection{Marginal distributions}\label{marginal-distributions}

This subsection explains how to recover the distribution of one variable
from the joint distribution.

The marginal distribution of \(X\) is obtained by summing or integrating
out \(Y\). Similarly, the marginal distribution of \(Y\) is obtained by
summing or integrating out \(X\).

For discrete random variables, {[} p\_X(x)=\sum\emph{y p}\{X,Y\}(x,y),
\qquad p\_Y(y)=\sum\emph{x p}\{X,Y\}(x,y). {]} For continuous random
variables, {[} f\_X(x)=\int\emph{\{-\infty\}\^{}\{\infty\}
f}\{X,Y\}(x,y),d y, \qquad f\_Y(y)=\int\emph{\{-\infty\}\^{}\{\infty\}
f}\{X,Y\}(x,y),d x. {]}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Common mistake}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

When finding \(f_X(x)\), integrate with respect to \(y\). When finding
\(f_Y(y)\), integrate with respect to \(x\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Discrete joint distribution example: two
dice}\label{discrete-joint-distribution-example-two-dice}

This subsection works out a full discrete joint distribution using two
dice.

\textbf{Example (Difference and maximum of two dice).}

Roll two fair dice. Let {[}
X=\text{absolute difference of the two values}, \qquad
Y=\text{maximum of the two values}. {]} Find the ranges, marginal pmfs,
and joint pmf table of \((X,Y)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The sample space has \(36\) equally likely outcomes \((i,j)\) with
\(i,j\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). The range of \(X\) is {[}
\mathbb{R}ange(X)=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}, {]} and the range of \(Y\) is {[}
\mathbb{R}ange(Y)=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}. {]}

For \(X=0\), the two dice match. There are \(6\) outcomes. For
\(X=d\ge 1\), the two dice differ by \(d\); there are \(2(6-d)\) ordered
outcomes. Hence {[}

\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
x&0&1&2&3&4&5\\ \hline
p_X(x)&6/36&10/36&8/36&6/36&4/36&2/36
\end{array}

{]}

For \(Y=y\), at least one die equals \(y\) and both dice are at most
\(y\). There are {[} y\textsuperscript{2-(y-1)}2=2y-1 {]} outcomes. Thus
{[}

\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
y&1&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline
p_Y(y)&1/36&3/36&5/36&7/36&9/36&11/36
\end{array}

{]}

The joint pmf table is {[}

\begin{array}{c|cccccc|c}
& X=0&X=1&X=2&X=3&X=4&X=5&p_Y(y)\\ \hline
Y=1&1/36&0&0&0&0&0&1/36\\
Y=2&1/36&2/36&0&0&0&0&3/36\\
Y=3&1/36&2/36&2/36&0&0&0&5/36\\
Y=4&1/36&2/36&2/36&2/36&0&0&7/36\\
Y=5&1/36&2/36&2/36&2/36&2/36&0&9/36\\
Y=6&1/36&2/36&2/36&2/36&2/36&2/36&11/36\\ \hline
p_X(x)&6/36&10/36&8/36&6/36&4/36&2/36&1
\end{array}

{]} The entries sum to \(1\), and the row and column sums agree with the
marginals.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Same marginals, different joint pmf).}

Show that marginal distributions alone do not determine the joint
distribution.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(X,Y\in\{0,1\}\), and suppose both marginals satisfy {[}
\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\frac12, \qquad
\mathbb{P}(Y=0)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=\frac12. {]} Consider the two joint pmf
tables {[}

\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &Y=0&Y=1\\ \hline
X=0&1/2&0\\
X=1&0&1/2
\end{array}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &Y=0&Y=1\\ \hline
X=0&1/4&1/4\\
X=1&1/4&1/4
\end{array}

. {]} Both tables have the same marginal distributions for \(X\) and
\(Y\). However, the dependence structure is different. In the first
table, \(Y=X\) always. In the second table, \(X\) and \(Y\) are
independent. Therefore marginals alone do not determine the joint
distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Continuous joint distribution
example}\label{continuous-joint-distribution-example}

This subsection gives a full continuous example with normalization, a
region probability, a marginal density, and a one-dimensional
probability.

\textbf{Example (A joint pdf on the unit square).}

A joint pdf is defined by {[} f(x,y)=6xy\^{}2,
\qquad 0\textless x\textless1,\quad 0\textless y\textless1, {]} and
\(f(x,y)=0\) otherwise.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Check that it is a valid joint pdf.
\item
  Calculate \(\mathbb{P}(X+Y\ge 1)\).
\item
  Calculate the marginal pdf of \(X\), \(f_X(x)\).
\item
  Calculate \(\mathbb{P}\left(\frac12<X<\frac34\right)\).
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{(1) Validity.} Clearly \(f(x,y)\ge 0\) on its support. Also, {[}
\int\_0\textsuperscript{1\int\_0}1 6xy\^{}2,d x,d y =\int\_0\^{}1
3y\^{}2,d y =\left.y\textsuperscript{3\right\textbar\_0}1=1. {]} Thus
\(f\) is a valid joint pdf.

\textbf{(2) Region probability.} The event \(X+Y\ge 1\) corresponds to
\(0<x<1\) and \(1-x\le y\le 1\). Hence {[} \mathbb{P}(X+Y\ge 1)
=\int\emph{0\textsuperscript{1\int\_\{1-x\}}\{1\}6xy\^{}2,d y,d x. {]}
Compute the inner integral: {[}
\int}\{1-x\}\textsuperscript{\{1\}6xy}2,d y
=2x\left(1-(1-x)\^{}3\right). {]} Therefore {[}
\mathbb{P}(X+Y\ge 1)=\int\_0\^{}1 2x\left(1-(1-x)\^{}3\right),d
x=\frac{9}{10}. {]}

\textbf{(3) Marginal of \(X\).} {[} f\_X(x)=\int\_0\^{}1 6xy\^{}2,d
y=6x\cdot \frac13=2x, \qquad 0\textless x\textless1. {]}

\textbf{(4) Probability for \(X\).} {[}
\mathbb{P}\left(\frac12\textless X\textless{}\frac34\right)=\int\_\{1/2\}\^{}\{3/4\}2x,d
x =\left.x\textsuperscript{2\right\textbar\_\{1/2\}}\{3/4\}
=\frac{9}{16}-\frac{4}{16}=\frac{5}{16}. {]} Thus {[}
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X+Y\ge1)=\frac{9}{10},\qquad f_X(x)=2x,
\qquad \mathbb{P}\left(\frac12<X<\frac34\right)=\frac{5}{16}.} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem (Marginal density practice).}

Suppose {[}
f(x,y)=c(x+y),\qquad 0\textless x\textless1,\quad 0\textless y\textless1,
{]} and \(0\) otherwise. Find \(c\), \(f_X(x)\), and
\(\mathbb{P}(X\le 1/2)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Normalize: {[} 1=\int\_0\textsuperscript{1\int\_0}1 c(x+y),d y,d x
=c\int\_0\^{}1\left(x+\frac12\right),d x
=c\left(\frac12+\frac12\right)=c. {]} So \(c=1\). Then {[}
f\_X(x)=\int\_0\^{}1(x+y),d y=x+\frac12, \qquad 0\textless x\textless1.
{]} Finally, {[}
\mathbb{P}(X\le 1/2)=\int\_0\^{}\{1/2\}\left(x+\frac12\right),d x
=\left.\left(\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\right)\right\textbar\_0\^{}\{1/2\}
=\frac18+\frac14=\frac38. {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Multivariate Normal
Distribution}\label{multivariate-normal-distribution}

This section introduces the most important multivariate continuous
distribution: the multivariate normal distribution.

\subsection{Definition and geometry}\label{definition-and-geometry}

This subsection defines the multivariate normal density and explains the
roles of the mean vector and covariance matrix.

\textbf{Definition (Multivariate normal distribution).}

Let {[} \vec X=

\begin{pmatrix}X_1\\ \vdots\\ X_d\end{pmatrix}

. {]} We say {[} \vec X\sim\mathbb{N}ormal(\vec\mu,\Sigma) {]} if
\(\vec\mu\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\Sigma\) is a \(d\times d\) symmetric
positive definite matrix, and the joint pdf is {[} f\_\{\vec X\}(\vec x)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d|\Sigma|}}
\exp\left[-\frac12(\vec x-\vec\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\vec x-\vec\mu)\right].
{]}

The mean vector is {[} \mathbb{E}{[}\vec X{]}=\vec\mu, {]} and the
covariance matrix is {[} \operatorname{Cov}(\vec X)=\Sigma. {]} The
matrix \(\Sigma\) controls the spread and orientation of the density. A
nearly diagonal covariance matrix produces contours aligned with the
coordinate axes; a covariance matrix with nonzero off-diagonal entries
produces tilted elliptical contours.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Visual idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Multivariate normal contours are ellipses. Diagonal covariance gives
axis-aligned contours, while nonzero covariance tilts the contours.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Covariance and
correlation}\label{covariance-and-correlation}

This subsection defines covariance and correlation as second-order
summaries of the relationship between two random variables.

\textbf{Definition (Covariance and correlation).}

For two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the covariance is {[}
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}{[}(X-\mathbb{E}{[}X{]})(Y-\mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}){]}
=\mathbb{E}{[}XY{]}-\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}\mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}. {]} The Pearson
correlation coefficient is {[}
\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{STD}(X)\operatorname{STD}(Y)}.
{]} It satisfies {[} -1\le \operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)\le 1. {]}

Covariance has units depending on \(X\) and \(Y\), while correlation is
dimensionless. Positive correlation means that large values of \(X\)
tend to occur with large values of \(Y\); negative correlation means
that large values of \(X\) tend to occur with small values of \(Y\).

\textbf{Example (Covariance from a small joint table).}

Let \(X,Y\in\{0,1\}\) with joint pmf {[}

\begin{array}{c|cc}
&Y=0&Y=1\\ \hline
X=0&0.40&0.10\\
X=1&0.10&0.40
\end{array}

. {]} Find \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The marginals are {[} \mathbb{P}(X=1)=0.10+0.40=0.50, \qquad
\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=0.10+0.40=0.50. {]} Thus
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]=0.5\). Also, since \(XY=1\) only when
\(X=1,Y=1\), {[} \mathbb{E}{[}XY{]}=\mathbb{P}(X=1,Y=1)=0.40. {]}
Therefore {[}
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}{[}XY{]}-\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}\mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}=0.40-(0.50)(0.50)=0.15.
{]} The covariance is positive.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Conditional Probability and Conditional
Distributions}\label{conditional-probability-and-conditional-distributions}

This section formalizes the idea of updating probabilities after some
information has been observed.

\subsection{Conditional probability for
events}\label{conditional-probability-for-events}

This subsection recalls the event-level definition from Section 1.

\textbf{Definition (Conditional probability).}

If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), then the probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is {[}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}. {]} When
\(B\) is fixed, \(\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid B)\) is another probability
measure.

\subsection{Conditional distributions}\label{conditional-distributions}

This subsection extends conditional probability from events to random
variables.

For two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the conditional pmf/pdf of
\(Y\) given \(X=x\) is {[}
p\_\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid x)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}, {]} provided
\(p_X(x)>0\). In the continuous case the same formula is written using
densities: {[} f\_\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}, {]}
provided \(f_X(x)>0\).

\textbf{Example (Triangle uniform distribution).}

Let \((X,Y)\) be uniformly distributed on the triangular region {[}
D=\{(x,y):x\ge0,~y\ge0,~x+y\le1\}. {]} The joint pdf is {[} f(x,y)=

\begin{cases}
2, & (x,y)\in D,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

{]} Find \(f_X(x)\) and \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For a fixed \(x\in[0,1]\), the variable \(y\) ranges from \(0\) to
\(1-x\). Hence {[} f\_X(x)=\int\emph{0\^{}\{1-x\}2,d y=2(1-x),
\qquad 0\le x\le 1. {]} Therefore {[} f}\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid x)
=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)} =\frac{2}{2(1-x)}=\frac{1}{1-x}, {]} for
\(0\le y\le 1-x\). Thus, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\) is uniform on
\([0,1-x]\): {[}
\boxed{f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{1-x},\qquad 0\le y\le 1-x.} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Beta-Bernoulli joint distribution).}

The Beta-Bernoulli model is a basic Bayesian model. Suppose {[}
Y\sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) {]} and, conditional on \(Y=y\),
{[} X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(y). {]} Find the joint
distribution \(p(x,y)\) and identify the posterior distribution of \(Y\)
given \(X=x\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The conditional pmf of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is {[}
p(x\mid y)=y\textsuperscript{x(1-y)}\{1-x\}, \qquad x\in\{0,1\}. {]} The
density of \(Y\) is {[}
f\_Y(y)=\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}y\textsuperscript{\{\alpha-1\}(1-y)}\{\beta-1\},
\qquad 0\textless y\textless1. {]} Thus the joint distribution is {[}
p(x,y)=p(x\mid y)f\_Y(y)
=\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}y\textsuperscript{\{\alpha+x-1\}(1-y)}\{\beta+1-x-1\}.
{]} As a function of \(y\) with \(x\) fixed, this has the kernel of a
beta density: {[}
y\textsuperscript{\{(\alpha+x)-1\}(1-y)}\{(\beta+1-x)-1\}. {]} Therefore
{[} \boxed{Y\mid X=x\sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+x,\,\beta+1-x).} {]}
This is why the beta distribution is called a conjugate prior for the
Bernoulli model.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem (Conditional density practice).}

Let {[} f(x,y)=8xy, \qquad 0\textless y\textless x\textless1, {]} and
\(0\) otherwise. Find \(f_X(x)\) and \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For a fixed \(x\in(0,1)\), \(y\) ranges from \(0\) to \(x\). Thus {[}
f\_X(x)=\int\emph{0\^{}x 8xy,d y=8x\cdot\frac{x^2}{2}=4x\^{}3,
\qquad 0\textless x\textless1. {]} Then {[}
f}\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid x)=\frac{8xy}{4x^3}=\frac{2y}{x^2},
\qquad 0\textless y\textless x. {]} The conditional density integrates
to one: {[} \int\_0\^{}x \frac{2y}{x^2},d y=1. {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Independence}\label{independence-1}

This section explains independence for events and for random variables,
and shows how independence simplifies joint distributions and
expectations.

\subsection{Independence for events}\label{independence-for-events}

This subsection recalls the event-level definition of independence.

\textbf{Definition (Independent events).}

Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if {[}
\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B). {]} If
\(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), this is equivalent to {[}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A) \qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)=\mathbb{P}(B). {]}

The interpretation is that knowing one event occurred does not change
the probability of the other event.

\subsection{Independent random
variables}\label{independent-random-variables}

This subsection defines independence using joint and marginal
distributions.

\textbf{Definition (Independent random variables).}

Discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if {[}
p\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=p\_X(x)p\_Y(y) {]} for all possible \(x\) and \(y\).
Continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if {[}
f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=f\_X(x)f\_Y(y) {]} for all \(x,y\).

Similarly, \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are mutually independent if their joint
pmf/pdf factors into the product of their marginal pmfs/pdfs.

\textbf{Example (Independent coin tosses).}

Toss a biased coin twice. Let {[} X=

\begin{cases}1,&\text{first toss is Heads},\\0,&\text{first toss is Tails},\end{cases}
\qquad

Y=

\begin{cases}1,&\text{second toss is Heads},\\0,&\text{second toss is Tails}.
\end{cases}

{]} Suppose \(\mathbb{P}(\text{Heads})=p\). Show that \(X\) and \(Y\)
are independent.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Because the two tosses are independent, the probability of any pair of
outcomes factors. For example, {[}
\mathbb{P}(X=1,Y=0)=\mathbb{P}(\text{Heads then Tails})=p(1-p). {]}
Also, {[} \mathbb{P}(X=1)=p, \qquad \mathbb{P}(Y=0)=1-p. {]} Hence {[}
\mathbb{P}(X=1,Y=0)=\mathbb{P}(X=1)\mathbb{P}(Y=0). {]} The same check
holds for the other three pairs \((0,0),(0,1),(1,1)\). Therefore \(X\)
and \(Y\) are independent.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Checking dependence in the two-dice example).}

In the two-dice example, \(X\) is the absolute difference and \(Y\) is
the maximum. Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent?

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Use one entry of the joint table. We have {[}
p\_\{X,Y\}(0,1)=\frac{1}{36}. {]} The marginals are {[}
p\_X(0)=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16, \qquad p\_Y(1)=\frac{1}{36}. {]} If \(X\)
and \(Y\) were independent, then {[}
p\_\{X,Y\}(0,1)=p\_X(0)p\_Y(1)=\frac16\cdot\frac1{36}=\frac1{216}. {]}
But \(1/36\ne 1/216\). Therefore {[}
\boxed{X\text{ and }Y\text{ are not independent}.} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Checking independence by
factorization}\label{checking-independence-by-factorization}

This subsection gives a useful theorem for checking independence without
explicitly computing both marginals first.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: Factorization criterion}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \((X,Y)\) have joint pmf or pdf \(f(x,y)\). Then \(X\) and \(Y\) are
independent if and only if there exist nonnegative functions \(g(x)\)
and \(h(y)\) such that {[} f(x,y)=g(x)h(y) {]} for every \((x,y)\) in
the support, and the support itself factors as a product of a set in
\(x\) and a set in \(y\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Factorized joint density).}

Suppose a joint density has the form {[}
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{384}x\textsuperscript{2y}4
e\textsuperscript{\{-x/2\}e}\{-y\},
\qquad x\textgreater0,\textbackslash{} y\textgreater0. {]} Determine
whether \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

We can write {[}
f(x,y)=\left(x\textsuperscript{2e}\{-x/2\}\right)\left(\frac{1}{384}y\textsuperscript{4e}\{-y\}\right)
=g(x)h(y), {]} where {[}
g(x)=x\textsuperscript{2e}\{-x/2\},\qquad h(y)=\frac{1}{384}y\textsuperscript{4e}\{-y\}.
{]} The support is also a product region: \(x>0\) and \(y>0\). Hence the
joint density factors into a function of \(x\) times a function of
\(y\), so \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Support matters}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A formula may look factorized, but if the support couples \(x\) and
\(y\), the variables may not be independent. For example, \(f(x,y)=2\)
on \(0<x<1\), \(0<y<1-x\) does not have a product support.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Independence and
information}\label{independence-and-information}

This subsection explains why independence is essential in
likelihood-based statistical inference.

Suppose we observe \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\{0,1\}\), where the observations
are independent and identically distributed as
\(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta)\). Then the joint pmf factors as {[}
p(x\_1,\ldots,x\_n;\theta)=p(x\_1;\theta)p(x\_2;\theta)\cdots p(x\_n;\theta).
{]} Taking logarithms gives {[}
\log p(x\_1,\ldots,x\_n;\theta)=\log p(x\_1;\theta)+\cdots+\log p(x\_n;\theta).
{]} Thus the log-likelihood is a sum of individual log-likelihood
contributions: {[}
\ell(\theta;x\_1,\ldots,x\_n)=\ell(\theta;x\_1)+\cdots+\ell(\theta;x\_n).
{]} This is the statistical meaning of the phrase: total information
equals the sum of individual information.

\section{Consequences of
Independence}\label{consequences-of-independence}

This section collects important algebraic consequences of independence
for expectation, variance, and moment generating functions.

\subsection{Expectations of products}\label{expectations-of-products}

This subsection gives the key expectation rule for independent
variables.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: Products of functions of independent random variables}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then for suitable functions \(g\)
and \(h\), {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}g(X)h(Y){]}=\mathbb{E}{[}g(X){]}\mathbb{E}{[}h(Y){]}. {]}
In particular, {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}XY{]}=\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}\mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}. {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For the continuous case, {[} \mathbb{E}{[}g(X)h(Y){]}
=\int\int g(x)h(y)f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y),d x,d y. {]} Independence gives
\(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\), so {[} \mathbb{E}{[}g(X)h(Y){]}
=\int\int g(x)h(y)f\_X(x)f\_Y(y),d x,d y =\left(\int g(x)f\_X(x),d
x\right) \left(\int h(y)f\_Y(y),d y\right). {]} Thus {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}g(X)h(Y){]}=\mathbb{E}{[}g(X){]}\mathbb{E}{[}h(Y){]}. {]}
The discrete proof is the same with sums replacing integrals.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Moment generating functions and
sums}\label{moment-generating-functions-and-sums}

This subsection explains why moment generating functions are especially
useful for sums of independent random variables.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: MGF of a sum of independent random variables}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent and \(Z=X+Y\), then {[}
M\_Z(t)=M\_X(t)M\_Y(t), {]} where \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By definition, {[}
M\_Z(t)=\mathbb{E}{[}e\^{}\{tZ\}{]}=\mathbb{E}{[}e\^{}\{t(X+Y)\}{]}=\mathbb{E}{[}e\textsuperscript{\{tX\}e}\{tY\}{]}.
{]} Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(e^{tX}\) and \(e^{tY}\) are
independent functions of them, so {[}
M\_Z(t)=\mathbb{E}{[}e\^{}\{tX\}{]}\mathbb{E}{[}e\^{}\{tY\}{]}=M\_X(t)M\_Y(t).
{]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: Sum of independent normal random variables}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Suppose {[} X\sim\mathbb{N}ormal(\mu\_1,\sigma\_1\^{}2), \qquad
Y\sim\mathbb{N}ormal(\mu\_2,\sigma\_2\^{}2), {]} and \(X\) and \(Y\) are
independent. Then {[}
X+Y\sim\mathbb{N}ormal(\mu\_1+\mu\_2,\sigma\_1\textsuperscript{2+\sigma\_2}2).
{]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The MGF of a normal random variable
\(X\sim\mathbb{N}ormal(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is {[}
M\_X(t)=\exp\left(\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2t^2}{2}\right). {]} Let \(Z=X+Y\).
Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, {[} M\_Z(t)=M\_X(t)M\_Y(t). {]}
Therefore {[} M\_Z(t) =\exp\left(\mu\_1t+\frac{\sigma_1^2t^2}{2}\right)
\exp\left(\mu\_2t+\frac{\sigma_2^2t^2}{2}\right). {]} Combining
exponents, {[}
M\_Z(t)=\exp\left((\mu\_1+\mu\_2)t+\frac{(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2}{2}\right),
{]} which is the MGF of
\(\mathbb{N}ormal(\mu_1+\mu_2,\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Linearity, covariance, and variance of
sums}\label{linearity-covariance-and-variance-of-sums}

This subsection separates what is always true from what requires
independence.

For any random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) on the same sample space, {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}aX+bY{]}=a\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}+b\mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}. {]} No
independence is required for linearity of expectation.

The variance of a linear combination is {[}
\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a\textsuperscript{2\operatorname{Var}(X)+b}2\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
{]} If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then {[}
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0, {]} and therefore {[}
\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a\textsuperscript{2\operatorname{Var}(X)+b}2\operatorname{Var}(Y).
{]}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Zero covariance is not the same as independence}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Independence implies zero covariance, provided the variances exist. The
converse is not true: zero covariance does not necessarily imply
independence.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem (A zero covariance but not independent
example).}

Let \(X\) take values \(-1,0,1\) with probabilities \(1/3,1/3,1/3\), and
define \(Y=X^2\). Show that \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0\) but \(X\) and
\(Y\) are not independent.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

We compute {[} \mathbb{E}{[}X{]}=\frac{-1+0+1}{3}=0, \qquad Y=X\^{}2,
\qquad XY=X\^{}3. {]} Thus {[}
\mathbb{E}{[}XY{]}=\mathbb{E}{[}X\^{}3{]}=\frac{(-1)^3+0^3+1^3}{3}=0.
{]} Hence {[}
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}{[}XY{]}-\mathbb{E}{[}X{]}\mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}=0-0\cdot \mathbb{E}{[}Y{]}=0.
{]} But \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent. For example, {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid X=0)=1, {]} while {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=0)=\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\frac13. {]} Knowing \(X=0\) changes the
probability of \(Y=0\), so \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Law of Total Probability and Bayes Theorem for Random
Variables}\label{law-of-total-probability-and-bayes-theorem-for-random-variables}

This section extends total probability and Bayes theorem from events to
random variables.

\subsection{Law of total probability for random
variables}\label{law-of-total-probability-for-random-variables}

This subsection shows how a marginal distribution can be obtained by
averaging conditional distributions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: Law of total probability for random variables}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

If \(X\) is discrete, then {[} p\_Y(y)=\sum\emph{\{x'\}
p}\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid x')p\_X(x'). {]} If \(X\) is continuous, then {[}
p\_Y(y)=\int p\_\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid x')p\_X(x'),d x'. {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Poisson-Binomial thinning).}

Let {[} X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda), \qquad
Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(x,p). {]} Find the marginal
distribution of \(Y\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By the law of total probability, {[} \mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\sum\emph{\{x\}
\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid X=x)\mathbb{P}(X=x). {]} Since
\(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(x,p)\), the sum starts at
\(x=y\): {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\sum}\{x\ge y\}\binom{x}{y}p\textsuperscript{y(1-p)}\{x-y\}\frac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}.
{]} Using \(\binom{x}{y}=x!/[y!(x-y)!]\), we get {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\sum\emph{\{x\ge y\}\frac{p^y(1-p)^{x-y}\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{y!(x-y)!}.
{]} Let \(k=x-y\). Then {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\frac{(\lambda p)^y e^{-\lambda}}{y!}
\sum}\{k=0\}\textsuperscript{\{\infty\}\textbackslash frac\{\left(\lambda(1-p)\right)}k\}\{k!\}.
{]} The sum is \(e^{\lambda(1-p)}\), so {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\frac{(\lambda p)^y e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda(1-p)}}{y!}
=\frac{(\lambda p)^y e^{-\lambda p}}{y!}. {]} Therefore {[}
\boxed{Y\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda p).} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Bayes theorem for random
variables}\label{bayes-theorem-for-random-variables}

This subsection gives Bayes theorem in pmf/pdf notation.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: Bayes theorem for random variables}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), {[} p\_\{X\mid Y\}(x\mid y)
=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)} =\frac{p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x)}{p_Y(y)}.
{]} If \(X\) is discrete, then {[} p\_\{X\mid Y\}(x\mid y)
=\frac{p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x)}{\sum_{x'}p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x')p_X(x')}.
{]} If \(X\) is continuous, then {[} p\_\{X\mid Y\}(x\mid y)
=\frac{p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x)}{\int p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x')p_X(x')\,d x'}.
{]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example (Bayesian update with a beta prior).}

Suppose \(Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) and
\(X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(y)\). Use Bayes theorem to find
\(Y\mid X=1\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By Bayes theorem, {[}
f\_\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid 1)\propto \mathbb{P}(X=1\mid Y=y)f\_Y(y). {]} Now
{[} \mathbb{P}(X=1\mid Y=y)=y, \qquad
f\_Y(y)\propto y\textsuperscript{\{\alpha-1\}(1-y)}\{\beta-1\}. {]}
Therefore {[}
f\_\{Y\mid X\}(y\mid 1)\propto y\textsuperscript{\{\alpha\}(1-y)}\{\beta-1\}.
{]} This is the kernel of \(\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+1,\beta)\), so
{[} \boxed{Y\mid X=1\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+1,\beta).} {]}
Similarly, if \(X=0\), then
\(Y\mid X=0\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta+1)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Practice Problem (Total probability practice).}

Suppose \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\) and {[}
Y\mid X=0\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p\_0), \qquad
Y\mid X=1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p\_1). {]} Find
\(\mathbb{P}(Y=1)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Use total probability over the two possible values of \(X\): {[}
\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X=0)\mathbb{P}(X=0)
+\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X=1)\mathbb{P}(X=1). {]} Since \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=q\)
and \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=1-q\), {[} \boxed{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=p_0(1-q)+p_1q.}
{]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Conditional Independence}\label{conditional-independence-1}

This section introduces conditional independence, a central concept in
Bayesian statistics, causal inference, and graphical models.

\subsection{Definition and equivalent
forms}\label{definition-and-equivalent-forms}

This subsection defines conditional independence and lists several
equivalent factorization properties.

\textbf{Definition (Conditional independence).}

Random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are conditionally independent given
\(Z\) if {[}
p\_\{X,Y\mid Z\}(x,y\mid z)=p\_\{X\mid Z\}(x\mid z)p\_\{Y\mid Z\}(y\mid z)
{]} for all relevant \(x,y,z\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem: Equivalent forms}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are conditionally independent given \(Z\), then the
following equivalent statements hold whenever the conditional densities
are defined:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  {[}
  p\_\{X,Y\mid Z\}(x,y\mid z)=p\_\{X\mid Z\}(x\mid z)p\_\{Y\mid Z\}(y\mid z).
  {]}
\item
  {[} p\_\{X\mid Y,Z\}(x\mid y,z)=p\_\{X\mid Z\}(x\mid z). {]}
\item
  {[} p\_\{X,Y,Z\}(x,y,z)=\frac{p_{X,Z}(x,z)p_{Y,Z}(y,z)}{p_Z(z)}. {]}
\item
  There exist functions \(g\) and \(h\) such that {[}
  p\_\{X,Y,Z\}(x,y,z)=g(x,z)h(y,z). {]}
\end{itemize}

\end{tcolorbox}

The key interpretation is: after \(Z\) is known, learning \(Y\) gives no
additional information about \(X\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Independence versus conditional independence}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Independence and conditional independence are different concepts.
Independence does not always imply conditional independence, and
conditional independence does not always imply independence.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Unit disk example}\label{unit-disk-example}

This subsection gives a full example involving a joint density on a
non-rectangular support.

\textbf{Example (Uniform distribution on the unit disk).}

Let \((X,Y)\) be uniformly distributed over the unit disk {[}
D=\{(x,y):x\textsuperscript{2+y}2\le1\}. {]} The joint pdf is {[}
f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=

\begin{cases}
c, & (x,y)\in D,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}

{]}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Find \(c\).
\item
  Find the marginal pdfs \(f_X(x)\) and \(f_Y(y)\).
\item
  Find the conditional pdf \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) for \(-1\le y\le1\).
\item
  Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{(a) Find \(c\).} Since the area of the unit disk is \(\pi\), {[}
1=\iint\_D c,d x,d y=c\cdot \pi. {]} Thus {[} \boxed{c=\frac1\pi.} {]}

\textbf{(b) Find the marginals.} For fixed \(x\in[-1,1]\), \(y\) ranges
from \(-\sqrt{1-x^2}\) to \(\sqrt{1-x^2}\). Hence {[}
f\_X(x)=\int\_\{-\sqrt{1-x^2}\}\textsuperscript{\{\textbackslash sqrt\{1-x}2\}\}\frac1\pi,d
y =\frac{2\sqrt{1-x^2}}{\pi}, \qquad -1\le x\le1. {]} By symmetry, {[}
f\_Y(y)=\frac{2\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\pi}, \qquad -1\le y\le1. {]}

\textbf{(c) Find the conditional pdf.} For fixed \(y\in[-1,1]\), \(x\)
ranges from \(-\sqrt{1-y^2}\) to \(\sqrt{1-y^2}\). Therefore {[}
f\_\{X\mid Y\}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}
=\frac{1/\pi}{2\sqrt{1-y^2}/\pi} =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-y^2}}, {]} for {[}
-\sqrt{1-y^2}\le x\le \sqrt{1-y^2}. {]} Thus {[} \boxed{
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{1-y^2}}, & -\sqrt{1-y^2}\le x\le \sqrt{1-y^2},\\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}} {]}

\textbf{(d) Independence.} If \(X\) and \(Y\) were independent, we would
have {[} f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=f\_X(x)f\_Y(y). {]} But inside the disk, {[}
f\_\{X,Y\}(x,y)=\frac1\pi, {]} whereas {[}
f\_X(x)f\_Y(y)=\frac{4\sqrt{(1-x^2)(1-y^2)}}{\pi^2}, {]} which is not
constant on the disk. Also, \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) depends on \(y\).
Therefore {[} \boxed{X\text{ and }Y\text{ are not independent}.} {]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Summary}\label{summary-1}

This section summarizes the main formulas and conceptual points from
joint and conditional probability.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Core formulas}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\begin{align*}
F_{X,Y}(x,y)&=\mathbb{P}(X\le x,Y\le y),\\
p_X(x)&=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y),\\
f_X(x)&=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,d y,\\
p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)&=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)},\\
p_Y(y)&=\sum_x p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x),\\
p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)&=\frac{p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x)}{p_Y(y)},\\
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)&=\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].
\end{align*}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Conceptual checklist}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A joint distribution contains the full relationship between variables.
\item
  A marginal distribution describes one variable after summing or
  integrating out the others.
\item
  A conditional distribution describes one variable after another
  variable has been fixed or observed.
\item
  Independence means the joint distribution factors into marginals.
\item
  Conditional independence means the conditional joint distribution
  factors after conditioning on another variable.
\item
  Bayes theorem reverses conditioning: it turns \(p_{Y\mid X}\) and
  \(p_X\) into \(p_{X\mid Y}\).
\end{itemize}

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Chapter 4: Expectations, Moments, and Moment Generating
Functions}\label{chapter-4-expectations-moments-and-moment-generating-functions}

This chapter develops numerical summaries of random variables and
introduces moment generating functions as a compact way to encode
moments and distributions.

\textbf{Topics.} Expected value; variance and standard deviation;
expectations of functions; moments; skewness; kurtosis; moment
generating functions; multivariate MGFs.

\section{Overview}\label{overview-1}

This section develops numerical summaries of random variables and
introduces moment generating functions as a compact way to encode
distributions.

In earlier sections, we described random variables by distributions:
CDFs, pmfs, and pdfs. In this section, we ask what numbers can summarize
a distribution. The most important summaries are expected value,
variance, and higher moments. Moment generating functions then package
all raw moments into one function, and they become especially powerful
for sums of independent random variables and normal distributions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Main message}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Expectation is the mathematical version of long-run average. Variance
measures spread. Higher moments describe shape. The moment generating
function, when it exists near \(0\), generates all moments and can
identify a distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Expected Value}\label{expected-value-1}

This section reviews the central idea of expectation and explains how it
connects probability theory with averages observed in data.

\subsection{Definition for discrete and continuous random
variables}\label{definition-for-discrete-and-continuous-random-variables}

This subsection gives the two most common formulas for expected value:
one for sums and one for integrals.

\textbf{Definition 1} (Expected value). Let \(X\) be a random variable.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  If \(X\) is discrete with pmf \(p_X(k)\), then
  \[\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{\text{all }k} k p_X(k).\]
\item
  If \(X\) is continuous with pdf \(f_X(x)\), then
  \[\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f_X(x)\,dx.\]
\end{itemize}

Expected value is a generalization of the concept ``average.'' It is not
necessarily the most likely value, and it does not need to be a value
that \(X\) can actually take. It is the weighted average of possible
values, where the weights are probabilities.

\textbf{Example 2} (Bernoulli random variable). Let
\(X\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), so
\[\mathbb{P}(X=0)=1-p,\qquad \mathbb{P}(X=1)=p.\] Find
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Using the definition of expectation for a discrete random variable,
\[\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_k k p_X(k)=0\cdot (1-p)+1\cdot p=p.\] Thus the mean
of a Bernoulli random variable is its success probability.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example 3} (Outcome of a fair die). Let \(X\) be the outcome of
rolling a fair six-sided die. Find \(\mathbb{E}[X]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here \(X\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) and each outcome has probability \(1/6\).
Therefore \[\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{k=1}^6 k\cdot \frac16
=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}=\frac{21}{6}=3.5.\] Notice that \(3.5\) is not a
possible die outcome. The expected value is a long-run average, not
necessarily a possible observation.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Operational meaning: long-run
average}\label{operational-meaning-long-run-average}

This subsection explains why the expected value is the number we expect
empirical averages to approach after many repeated trials.

Suppose we measure a random variable \(X\) in \(n\) independent trials
and record \[X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n.\] The sample average is
\[\overline X_n=\frac{1}{n}(X_1+\cdots+X_n).\] The operational meaning
of expected value is that \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) is the long-run average
value of repeated measurements of \(X\). Later, the Law of Large Numbers
will make this statement precise:
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\overline X_n=\mathbb{E}[X]\] in an appropriate
probabilistic sense.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Interpretation}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

If a casino game has expected gain \(-0.05\) dollars per play, then one
play can be positive or negative, but over many plays the average gain
per play tends to be close to \(-0.05\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Linearity of expectation}\label{linearity-of-expectation}

This subsection presents one of the most useful properties in
probability: expectation is linear.

\textbf{Theorem 4} (Linearity for one random variable). \emph{For
constants \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), \[\mathbb{E}[aX+b]=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b.\]}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Proof.} For the discrete case,
\[\mathbb{E}[aX+b]=\sum_x (ax+b)p_X(x)
=a\sum_x xp_X(x)+b\sum_x p_X(x)=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b.\] The continuous case
is the same argument with integrals:
\[\mathbb{E}[aX+b]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (ax+b)f_X(x)\,dx
=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b.\]~◻
\end{proof}

\textbf{Theorem 5} (Linearity for multiple random variables). \emph{For
any random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) defined on the same probability
space, \[\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y].\] This is true
whether or not \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Common mistake}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Linearity says \(\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]\). It
does \emph{not} say \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=g(\mathbb{E}[X])\) for a
nonlinear function \(g\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example 6} (Linearity without independence). Let \(X\) be any
random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[X]=3\), and let \(Y=2X+1\). Find
\(\mathbb{E}[4X-5Y]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Even though \(X\) and \(Y\) are clearly dependent, linearity still
applies. First, \[\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[2X+1]=2\mathbb{E}[X]+1=7.\]
Therefore,
\[\mathbb{E}[4X-5Y]=4\mathbb{E}[X]-5\mathbb{E}[Y]=4(3)-5(7)=12-35=-23.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Variance and Standard
Deviation}\label{variance-and-standard-deviation-1}

This section introduces variance as a measurement of spread around the
expected value.

\subsection{Definition and calculation
formula}\label{definition-and-calculation-formula}

This subsection gives both the conceptual definition and the
computational formula for variance.

\textbf{Definition 7} (Variance and standard deviation). The variance of
a random variable \(X\) is
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}\big[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\big].\] The
standard deviation is
\[\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.\]

Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean. It measures how
spread out the distribution is. Standard deviation puts the measurement
back into the original units of \(X\).

\textbf{Proposition 8} (Computational formula).
\emph{\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\big(\mathbb{E}[X]\big)^2.\]}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Proof.} Let \(\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]\). Then
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb{E}[X^2-2\mu X+\mu^2]
=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-2\mu\mathbb{E}[X]+\mu^2.\] Since \(\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]\),
this becomes
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-2\mu^2+\mu^2=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2.\]~◻
\end{proof}

\textbf{Proposition 9} (Scaling and shifting). \emph{For constants
\(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).\]}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Proof.} Since \(\mathbb{E}[aX+b]=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\),
\[(aX+b)-\mathbb{E}[aX+b]=aX+b-(a\mathbb{E}[X]+b)=a(X-\mathbb{E}[X]).\]
Therefore,
\[\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=\mathbb{E}\left[a^2(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\right]=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).\]~◻
\end{proof}

\textbf{Example 10} (Variance of a Bernoulli random variable). Let
\(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\). Find \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(X\) takes values \(0\) and \(1\), we have \(X^2=X\). Therefore
\[\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X]=p.\] Using the computational formula,
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}[X])^2=p-p^2=p(1-p).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example 11} (Variance of a fair die). Let \(X\) be the outcome
of rolling a fair six-sided die. Find \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

We already know \(\mathbb{E}[X]=3.5=7/2\). Next,
\[\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\frac{1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2+5^2+6^2}{6}
=\frac{91}{6}.\] Thus
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{91}{6}-\left(\frac72\right)^2
=\frac{91}{6}-\frac{49}{4}
=\frac{182-147}{12}=\frac{35}{12}.\] So the standard deviation is
\[\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\frac{35}{12}}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Expectation of a Function}\label{expectation-of-a-function}

This section explains how to compute the expectation of a transformed
random variable without first finding the full distribution of the
transformed variable.

\subsection{The law of the unconscious
statistician}\label{the-law-of-the-unconscious-statistician}

This subsection introduces a practical formula: to compute
\(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\), average \(g(x)\) with respect to the distribution
of \(X\).

Suppose \(Y=g(X)\). One way to compute \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) is to first
find the distribution of \(Y\) and then sum or integrate over \(Y\).
Often this is unnecessary.

\textbf{Theorem 12} (Expectation of a function). \emph{Let \(Y=g(X)\).}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \emph{If \(X\) is discrete, then
  \[\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x).\]}
\item
  \emph{If \(X\) is continuous, then
  \[\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)f_X(x)\,dx.\]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Proof idea for the discrete case.} Let the possible values of
\(X\) be \(x_k\). Then \[\mathbb{E}[Y]=\sum_y y\mathbb{P}(Y=y)
=\sum_y y\sum_{k:g(x_k)=y}\mathbb{P}(X=x_k).\] Since \(y=g(x_k)\) on the
event \(\{g(X)=y\}\),
\[\mathbb{E}[Y]=\sum_k g(x_k)\mathbb{P}(X=x_k).\]~◻
\end{proof}

\textbf{Example 13} (Computing a second moment directly). Let \(X\) be
the outcome of a fair six-sided die. Use the function formula to compute
\(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here \(g(x)=x^2\) and \(p_X(x)=1/6\) for \(x=1,2,3,4,5,6\). Therefore
\[\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\sum_{x=1}^6 x^2\frac16
=\frac{1+4+9+16+25+36}{6}=\frac{91}{6}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example 14} (Uniform distribution). Let
\(X\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Compute \(\mathbb{E}[X^m]\) for
an integer \(m\ge 1\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The pdf is \(f_X(x)=1\) for \(0\le x\le 1\). Thus
\[\mathbb{E}[X^m]=\int_0^1 x^m\,dx=\frac{1}{m+1}.\] In particular,
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=1/2\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=1/3\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Important distinction}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

In general, \[\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\ne g(\mathbb{E}[X]).\] For example, if
\(X\) is not constant, then \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\ne (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\) in
general. Their difference is the variance.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Products of independent random
variables}\label{products-of-independent-random-variables}

This subsection records the special multiplication rule for independent
variables.

\textbf{Theorem 15} (Expectation of products under independence).
\emph{If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then
\[\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].\] More generally, for
suitable functions \(f\) and \(g\),
\[\mathbb{E}[f(X)g(Y)]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\mathbb{E}[g(Y)].\]}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 16}. The converse is not true in general. The equality
\(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]\) only says \(X\) and \(Y\)
are uncorrelated; it does not necessarily imply independence.

\end{tcolorbox}

\textbf{Example 17} (Independent Bernoulli variables). Let
\(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) and
\(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\) be independent. Find
\(\mathbb{E}[XY]\).
