\(X\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), use the identity with
\(g(x)=x^2\) to compute \(\mathbb{E}[X^3]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The Poisson identity gives
\[\mathbb{E}[\lambda X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)^2].\] Expanding the
right-hand side, \[X(X-1)^2=X(X^2-2X+1)=X^3-2X^2+X.\] Therefore
\[\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^3]-2\mathbb{E}[X^2]+\mathbb{E}[X].\]
Solving for \(\mathbb{E}[X^3]\) gives
\[\mathbb{E}[X^3]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^2]+2\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X].\]
For \(X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \[\mathbb{E}[X]=\lambda,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\operatorname{Var}(X)+(\mathbb{E}X)^2=\lambda+\lambda^2.\]
Thus \[\mathbb{E}[X^3]
=\lambda(\lambda+\lambda^2)+2(\lambda+\lambda^2)-\lambda
=\lambda^3+3\lambda^2+\lambda.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-caution-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-caution-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-caution-color}{\faFire}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 45} (Use Jensen for a moment bound). Let \(X\)
be any random variable with finite fourth moment. Prove that
\[(\mathbb{E}[X^2])^2\leq \mathbb{E}[X^4].\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Apply Jensen's inequality to the convex function \(g(u)=u^2\) and the
random variable \(U=X^2\). Then
\[\mathbb{E}[g(U)]\geq g(\mathbb{E}[U]).\] This means
\[\mathbb{E}[(X^2)^2]\geq (\mathbb{E}[X^2])^2.\] Hence
\[\mathbb{E}[X^4]\geq (\mathbb{E}[X^2])^2.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Summary and Study Guide}\label{summary-and-study-guide-1}

This final section summarizes the main inequalities and indicates when
each one is useful.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Tool
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Statement / idea
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Uses
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Boole & \(\mathbb{P}(\cup_i E_i)\leq \sum_i\mathbb{P}(E_i)\) & At least
one bad event \\
Inclusion-exclusion & Exact alternating formula for finite unions &
Exact union probabilities \\
Bonferroni & Truncated inclusion-exclusion gives upper/lower bounds &
Better union bounds \\
Markov & \(\mathbb{P}(X\geq a)\leq \mathbb{E}[X]/a\) for \(X\geq0\) &
First moment tail bounds \\
Chebyshev &
\(\mathbb{P}(|X-\mathbb{E}X|\geq k)\leq \operatorname{Var}(X)/k^2\) &
Variance-based concentration \\
Chernoff & \(\mathbb{P}(X\geq a)\leq \inf_{t\geq0}e^{-ta}M_X(t)\) &
Exponential tail bounds \\
Hoeffding &
\(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X-\mathbb{E}\bar X|\geq\epsilon)\leq 2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}\)
for \(0\leq X_i\leq1\) & Bounded sample means \\
Cauchy-Schwarz &
\((\mathbb{E}[XY])^2\leq \mathbb{E}[X^2]\mathbb{E}[Y^2]\) & Correlation
and inner products \\
Hölder &
\(\mathbb{E}|XY|\leq (\mathbb{E}|X|^p)^{1/p}(\mathbb{E}|Y|^q)^{1/q}\) &
General moment control \\
Minkowski & \(\|X+Y\|_p\leq \|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p\) & Triangle inequality for
random variables \\
Jensen & \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\leq \mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) for convex \(g\) &
Convexity and expectation \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Main message}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

How to choose a bound Use Boole/Bonferroni for unions of events. Use
Markov if only a first moment is available. Use Chebyshev if a variance
is available. Use Chernoff or Hoeffding for exponential concentration,
especially for sums or averages of independent random variables. Use
Cauchy-Schwarz/Holder/Minkowski/Jensen when the problem involves
expectations of functions, products, or convexity.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Chapter 8: Sampling and Order
Statistics}\label{chapter-8-sampling-and-order-statistics}

This chapter moves from individual random variables to random samples.
The central idea is that statistics such as the sample mean, sample
variance, minimum, maximum, median, and range are themselves random
variables before the data are observed. Their distributions are called
\textbf{sampling distributions}.

\textbf{Topics.} Random samples; statistics and sampling distributions;
sample mean and sample variance; sums of random samples; convolution;
sampling from the normal distribution; chi-square, Student's \(t\), and
\(F\) distributions; order statistics; sample range and median.

\section{Overview}\label{overview-5}

This section moves from single random variables to random samples, which
are the mathematical objects behind statistical inference.

A statistical data set is usually modeled as a collection of random
variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\). The most important case is that the
variables are independent and identically distributed. From a random
sample we build statistics such as the sample mean, sample variance,
maximum, minimum, median, and sample range. The probability
distributions of these statistics are called sampling distributions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Main message}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A random sample produces random summaries. Statistical inference studies
the distributions of those summaries.
\[X_1,\ldots,X_n \quad \longrightarrow \quad T(X_1,\ldots,X_n).\] The
distribution of \(T\) tells us how the statistic behaves before the data
are observed.

\end{tcolorbox}

The key objects in this section are:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  random samples and iid assumptions;
\item
  sample mean \(\overline X\) and sample variance \(S^2\);
\item
  sums of independent variables and convolutions;
\item
  normal sampling theory: chi-square, \(t\), and \(F\) distributions;
\item
  order statistics \(X_{(1)}<\cdots<X_{(n)}\).
\end{itemize}

\section{Random Samples}\label{random-samples}

This section defines the random-sample model and explains why
independence is a modeling assumption, not automatic from the word
``sample.''

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 1} (Independent and identically distributed random
variables). Suppose \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are mutually independent random
variables and the marginal pdf or pmf of each \(X_i\) is the same
function \(f(x)\). Then \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are called
\textbf{independent and identically distributed}, abbreviated
\textbf{iid}, with pdf or pmf \(f(x)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 2} (Random sample). If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are iid
from a population distribution with pdf or pmf \(f(x)\), then
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is called a \textbf{random sample of size \(n\)} from
the population \(f(x)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are a random sample from \(f\), then their joint
density or mass function factors as \[f_{X_1,\ldots,X_n}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
 = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i).\] This product form is one of the main reasons
random samples are mathematically tractable.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 3} (Exponential lifetime sample). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\)
be a random sample from the exponential population
\[f(x;\beta)=\frac{1}{\beta}e^{-x/\beta},\qquad x>0,\ \beta>0.\] In an
engineering application, \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) might be the lifetimes, in
years, of \(n\) identical lightbulbs placed on test and used until
failure. Find the joint pdf of the sample.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are iid, the joint pdf is the product of the
marginal pdfs: \[f(x_1,\ldots,x_n;\beta)
 =\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\beta}e^{-x_i/\beta}
 =\frac{1}{\beta^n}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right),\]
for \(x_1>0,\ldots,x_n>0\), and \(0\) otherwise.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{How random samples arise}\label{how-random-samples-arise}

This subsection explains two common mechanisms that produce iid random
variables.

A random sample \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) can be obtained when:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  the population is effectively infinite and each observation is
  independently selected;
\item
  sampling is done \textbf{with replacement} from a finite population.
  Sampling with replacement is also the basis of the bootstrap idea.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Sampling without
replacement}\label{sampling-without-replacement}

This subsection emphasizes that sampling without replacement from a
finite population usually destroys independence.

Suppose the finite population is \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\). If we sample
without replacement, then the first and second draws are not
independent. For distinct population elements \(x\) and \(y\),
\[\mathbb{P}(X_1=x)=\frac{1}{N},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X_2=y\mid X_1=x)=\frac{1}{N-1}.\] Also,
\[\mathbb{P}(X_2=y\mid X_1=y)=0,\] because the value \(y\) cannot be
drawn again after it has already been selected.

Thus \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are not independent. However, they have the
same marginal distribution. When \(N\) is very large and \(n\) is small
compared with \(N\), sampling without replacement may be approximately
treated as independent.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 4} (Sampling without replacement). A population
consists of \(\{1,2,3,4\}\). Two values are sampled without replacement.
Let \(X_1\) be the first draw and \(X_2\) the second draw. Are \(X_1\)
and \(X_2\) independent?

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

No.~For example, \[\mathbb{P}(X_2=1)=\frac14,\] but
\[\mathbb{P}(X_2=1\mid X_1=1)=0.\] Because the conditional probability
differs from the marginal probability, \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are not
independent.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Statistics and Sampling
Distributions}\label{statistics-and-sampling-distributions}

This section introduces statistics as functions of random samples and
defines the sampling distribution of a statistic.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 5} (Statistic). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random
sample from a population. A \textbf{statistic} is any function of the
sample: \[Y=T(X_1,\ldots,X_n).\] The distribution of \(Y\) is called the
\textbf{sampling distribution} of the statistic \(T\).

\end{tcolorbox}

After the data are observed, we use lower-case letters
\(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) for the observed values. The statistic
\(T(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is random before the data are observed, while
\(T(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is the realized numerical value after observation.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 6} (Statistics). Each of the following is a statistic:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \(T=\max{X_1,\ldots,X_n}\);
\item
  \(T=\min{X_1,\ldots,X_n}\);
\item
  \(T=\overline X\);
\item
  \(T=S^2\);
\item
  \(T=3\).
\end{enumerate}

The last example is a strange statistic because it ignores the data, but
it is still a function of the sample.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A statistic only needs to be a function of the random sample. It does
not need to be useful. Therefore a constant such as \(T=3\) is
technically a statistic, although it contains no information about the
population.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Sample mean and sample
variance}\label{sample-mean-and-sample-variance}

This subsection introduces the two most common statistics in the course.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 7} (Sample mean). The \textbf{sample mean} is
\[\overline X=\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.\] For
observed values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the observed sample mean is
\[\overline x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 8} (Sample variance and sample standard deviation).
The \textbf{sample variance} is
\[S^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\overline X)^2.\] The
\textbf{sample standard deviation} is \(S=\sqrt{S^2}\). Observed values
are denoted by \(s^2\) and \(s\).

\end{tcolorbox}

Two useful algebraic formulas for observed values are
\[\min_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-a)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline x)^2,\]
and \[(n-1)s^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline x)^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-n\overline x^{\,2}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Proposition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Proposition 9} (Least-squares property of the sample mean).
\emph{For fixed observed values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the function
\[Q(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-a)^2\] is minimized at \(a=\overline x\).}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} Expand and differentiate:
\[Q(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-2a\sum_{i=1}^n x_i+na^2.\] Then
\[Q'(a)=-2\sum_{i=1}^n x_i+2na.\] Setting \(Q'(a)=0\) gives
\[a=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=\overline x.\] Also \(Q''(a)=2n>0\), so this
critical point is a minimum.~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Proposition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Proposition 10} (Computational formula for sample variance).
\emph{For observed data \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\),
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline x)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-n\overline x^{\,2}.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} Using \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=n\overline x\), \[\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline x)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_i^2-2\overline x x_i+\overline x^{\,2}\right)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-2\overline x\sum_{i=1}^n x_i+n\overline x^{\,2}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-2n\overline x^{\,2}+n\overline x^{\,2}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2-n\overline x^{\,2}.
\end{aligned}\]~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Mean and variance of the sample
mean}\label{mean-and-variance-of-the-sample-mean}

This subsection explains why \(\overline X\) estimates the population
mean and why its variance decreases as the sample size increases.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 11} (Basic properties of \(\overline X\) and \(S^2\)).
\emph{Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from a population with
mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Then
\[\mathbb{E}[\overline X]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[S^2]=\sigma^2.\] Thus \(\overline X\) is an unbiased
estimator of \(\mu\), and \(S^2\) is an unbiased estimator of
\(\sigma^2\).}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} By linearity of expectation, \[\mathbb{E}[\overline X]
=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right]
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_i]
=\frac1n(n\mu)=\mu.\] Since the observations are independent,
\[\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)
=\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)
=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.\] For the sample variance,
use
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\overline X)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mu)^2-n(\overline X-\mu)^2.\]
Taking expectations gives
\[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\overline X)^2\right]
=n\sigma^2-n\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)
=n\sigma^2-n\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
=(n-1)\sigma^2.\] Therefore \[\mathbb{E}[S^2]
=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\overline X)^2\right]
=\sigma^2.\]~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 12} (Unbiasedness check). Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be iid with mean \(10\) and variance \(4\). Find
\(\mathbb{E}[\overline X]\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)\), and
\(\mathbb{E}[S^2]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Using the theorem, \[\mathbb{E}[\overline X]=10,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)=\frac{4}{n},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[S^2]=4.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Sums of Random Samples}\label{sums-of-random-samples}

This section studies how the distribution of a sum, and therefore the
sample mean, can be derived from the distribution of the original
sample.

Let \[Y=X_1+\cdots+X_n,
\qquad
\overline X=\frac{Y}{n}.\] If the pdf of \(Y\) is \(f_Y\), then the pdf
of \(\overline X=Y/n\) is \[f_{\overline X}(x)=n f_Y(nx).\] This follows
from the one-dimensional change-of-variables formula.

\subsection{MGF method}\label{mgf-method}

This subsection uses moment generating functions to identify the
distribution of sums and sample means.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 13} (MGF of the sample mean). \emph{Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from a population with moment
generating function \(M_X(t)\). Then
\[M_{\overline X}(t)=\left[M_X\left(\frac{t}{n}\right)\right]^n.\]
Equivalently, for the sum \(Y=X_1+\cdots+X_n\),
\[M_Y(t)=\left[M_X(t)\right]^n.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} By independence,
\[M_Y(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{t(X_1+\cdots+X_n)}]
=\prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[e^{tX_i}]
=\left[M_X(t)\right]^n.\] Since \(\overline X=Y/n\),
\[M_{\overline X}(t)
=\mathbb{E}[e^{tY/n}]
=M_Y(t/n)
=\left[M_X(t/n)\right]^n.\]~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 14} (Normal sample mean). Suppose
\(X_i\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) for
\(i=1,\ldots,n\). Find the distribution of \(\overline X\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The MGF of \(X_i\) is
\[M_X(t)=\exp\left(\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2t^2}{2}\right).\] Thus
\[\begin{aligned}
M_{\overline X}(t)
&=\left[M_X(t/n)\right]^n\\
&=\left[\exp\left(\mu\frac{t}{n}+\frac{\sigma^2(t/n)^2}{2}\right)\right]^n\\
&=\exp\left(\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2n}\right).
\end{aligned}\] This is the MGF of
\(\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\). Therefore
\[\overline X\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 15} (Gamma sample mean). Suppose
\(X_i\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)\),
where \(\beta\) is the rate parameter, so
\[M_X(t)=\left(\frac{\beta}{\beta-t}\right)^\alpha,
\qquad t<\beta.\] Find the distribution of \(\overline X\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

First, \[Y=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(n\alpha,\beta),\]
because the MGF of \(Y\) is
\[M_Y(t)=\left(\frac{\beta}{\beta-t}\right)^{n\alpha}.\] Since
\(\overline X=Y/n\), \[M_{\overline X}(t)=M_Y(t/n)
=\left(\frac{\beta}{\beta-t/n}\right)^{n\alpha}
=\left(\frac{n\beta}{n\beta-t}\right)^{n\alpha}.\] Therefore
\[\overline X\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(n\alpha,n\beta)\] under the rate
parameterization. Under a scale parameterization \(\theta=1/\beta\),
this is \[\overline X\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(n\alpha,\theta/n).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Convolution method}\label{convolution-method}

This subsection gives the general integral formula for the density of a
sum of independent continuous random variables.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 16} (Convolution formula). \emph{If \(X\) and \(Y\) are
independent continuous random variables with pdfs \(f_X\) and \(f_Y\),
then the pdf of \(Z=X+Y\) is
\[f_Z(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(w)f_Y(z-w)\,dw.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} Let \[Z=X+Y,
\qquad
W=X.\] Then \[X=W,
\qquad
Y=Z-W.\] The Jacobian determinant of the inverse transformation
\((z,w)\mapsto (x,y)=(w,z-w)\) has absolute value \(1\). Hence
\[f_{Z,W}(z,w)=f_{X,Y}(w,z-w)=f_X(w)f_Y(z-w).\] Integrating out \(w\)
gives \[f_Z(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(w)f_Y(z-w)\,dw.\]~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 17} (Sum of two exponential random variables). Let
\(X,Y\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), so
\(f_X(x)=e^{-x}\) for \(x\geq0\). Find the pdf of \(Z=X+Y\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(z>0\), \[f_Z(z)=\int_{0}^{z}e^{-w}e^{-(z-w)}\,dw
=\int_0^z e^{-z}\,dw
=ze^{-z}.\] For \(z\leq0\), \(f_Z(z)=0\). Therefore
\[f_Z(z)=ze^{-z}\mathbf{1}_{\{z>0\}},\] which is a gamma density with
shape \(2\) and rate \(1\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 18} (Sum of Cauchy random variables). Suppose \(U\) and
\(V\) are independent Cauchy random variables:
\[U\sim \operatorname{Cauchy}(0,\sigma),
\qquad
V\sim \operatorname{Cauchy}(0,\tau),\] with pdfs
\[f_U(u)=\frac{1}{\pi\sigma}\frac{1}{1+(u/\sigma)^2},
\qquad
f_V(v)=\frac{1}{\pi\tau}\frac{1}{1+(v/\tau)^2}.\] Find the distribution
of \(Z=U+V\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By convolution, \[f_Z(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{1}{\pi\sigma}\frac{1}{1+(w/\sigma)^2}
\frac{1}{\pi\tau}\frac{1}{1+((z-w)/\tau)^2}\,dw.\] A standard Cauchy
convolution calculation gives
\[f_Z(z)=\frac{1}{\pi(\sigma+\tau)}\frac{1}{1+(z/(\sigma+\tau))^2}.\]
Thus \[Z=U+V\sim \operatorname{Cauchy}(0,\sigma+\tau).\] This is an
important example showing that averaging Cauchy variables does not
produce a distribution with smaller spread in the usual variance sense;
the Cauchy distribution does not have a finite mean or variance.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 19} (Convolution practice). Let
\(X,Y\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Use
convolution to find the pdf of \(Z=X+Y\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(0<z<1\), \[f_Z(z)=\int_0^z 1\,dw=z.\] For \(1\leq z<2\),
\[f_Z(z)=\int_{z-1}^{1}1\,dw=2-z.\] Thus \[f_Z(z)=
\begin{cases}
z, &0<z<1,\\
2-z, &1\leq z<2,\\
0, &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Sampling from the Normal
Distribution}\label{sampling-from-the-normal-distribution}

This section presents the central normal-sampling facts that lead to the
chi-square, Student's \(t\), and \(F\) distributions.

\subsection{Normal sample mean and sample
variance}\label{normal-sample-mean-and-sample-variance}

This subsection states the special independence and chi-square results
that hold only for normal samples.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 20} (Normal sampling theorem). \emph{Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from
\(\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Then}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \emph{\(\overline X\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu,\sigma^2/n\right)\);}
\item
  \emph{\(\overline X\) and \(S^2\) are independent;}
\item
  \emph{\[\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_{n-1}.\]}
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Why this theorem matters}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The theorem says that for normal samples, uncertainty about the mean and
uncertainty about the variance separate cleanly. This is the starting
point for the \(t\) distribution, confidence intervals, and many
classical tests.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Chi-square random
variables}\label{chi-square-random-variables}

This subsection reviews the chi-square distribution and its relationship
with squared standard normals.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 21} (Chi-square facts). \emph{The chi-square
distribution with \(k\) degrees of freedom is a gamma distribution:
\[\chi_k^2\sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha=\frac{k}{2},\theta=2\right),\]
where \(\theta\) is the scale parameter. Also:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \emph{If \(Z\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,1)\), then
  \(Z^2\sim \chi^2_1\).}
\item
  \emph{If \(X_i\sim\chi^2_{p_i}\) are independent, then
  \[X_1+\cdots+X_n\sim \chi^2_{p_1+\cdots+p_n}.\]}
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof sketch.} If \(Z\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,1)\), then by the
transformation \(Y=Z^2\), the density of \(Y\) is
\[f_Y(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}e^{-y/2},\qquad y>0,\] which is
\(\operatorname{Gamma}(1/2,2)\), hence \(\chi_1^2\). The sum property
follows from multiplying MGFs. The MGF of \(\chi_k^2\) is
\((1-2t)^{-k/2}\), and products of such MGFs add the degrees of
freedom.~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 22} (Normal sample variance). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_{10}\)
be a random sample from \(\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). What is
the distribution of \(9S^2/\sigma^2\)?

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By the normal sampling theorem,
\[\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_{n-1}.\] With \(n=10\),
\[\frac{9S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_9.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Student's \(t\)
distribution}{Student's t distribution}}\label{students-t-distribution}

This subsection introduces the distribution used when the population
variance is unknown.

This topic was first addressed by W. S. Gosset, who published under the
pseudonym \emph{Student}, in the early 1900s.

If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is a random sample from a normal population with
mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and if \(\sigma^2\) is known,
then
\[\frac{\overline X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,1).\]
When \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we replace \(\sigma\) by the sample
standard deviation \(S\) and study
\[T=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 23} (Student's \(t\) distribution). Let
\(U\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,1)\) and \(V\sim \chi^2_p\) be
independent. Then \[T=\frac{U}{\sqrt{V/p}}\] has a \textbf{Student's
\(t\) distribution} with \(p\) degrees of freedom, denoted \(t_p\).

\end{tcolorbox}

For a normal sample, \[\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}
=\frac{(\overline X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)}{\sqrt{{(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2}/(n-1)}}
\sim t_{n-1}.\]

The pdf of \(T\sim t_p\) is
\[f_T(t)=\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{p+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{p\pi}\,\Gamma\left(\frac p2\right)}
\left(1+\frac{t^2}{p}\right)^{-(p+1)/2},
\qquad -\infty<t<\infty.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 24}. If \(p=1\), the Student's \(t\) distribution becomes
the Cauchy distribution. The \(t\) distribution has heavier tails than
the normal distribution. It has no MGF because it does not have moments
of all orders. If \(T\sim t_p\), then only moments of order less than
\(p\) exist. In particular, \[\mathbb{E}[T]=0 \quad \text{for } p>1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{p}{p-2}\quad \text{for } p>2.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 25} (Constructing a \(t\) statistic). Suppose
\(X_1,\ldots,X_{16}\) are iid \(\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
Find the distribution of \[T=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/4}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(n=16\), \(\sqrt n=4\). Therefore
\[T=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}=t_{15}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{\(F\)
distribution}{F distribution}}\label{f-distribution}

This subsection introduces the distribution of a ratio of scaled
independent chi-square random variables, which is used to compare
variances.

Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from
\(\operatorname{Normal}(\mu_X,\sigma_X^2)\), and let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\)
be an independent random sample from
\(\operatorname{Normal}(\mu_Y,\sigma_Y^2)\). Then
\[\frac{(n-1)S_X^2}{\sigma_X^2}\sim \chi^2_{n-1},
\qquad
\frac{(m-1)S_Y^2}{\sigma_Y^2}\sim \chi^2_{m-1}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 26} (\(F\) distribution). If \(U\sim\chi^2_p\) and
\(V\sim\chi^2_q\) are independent, then \[F=\frac{U/p}{V/q}\] has an
\textbf{\(F\) distribution} with \(p\) and \(q\) degrees of freedom,
denoted \(F_{p,q}\).

\end{tcolorbox}

Thus \[\frac{S_X^2/\sigma_X^2}{S_Y^2/\sigma_Y^2}
\sim F_{n-1,m-1}.\] The pdf of \(F\sim F_{p,q}\) is, for \(x>0\),
\[f_F(x)=
\frac{1}{B(p/2,q/2)}
\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)^{p/2}
\frac{x^{p/2-1}}{\left(1+\frac{p}{q}x\right)^{(p+q)/2}}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 27} (Basic relationships for the \(F\) distribution).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \emph{If \(X\sim F_{p,q}\), then \(1/X\sim F_{q,p}\).}
\item
  \emph{If \(T\sim t_q\), then \(T^2\sim F_{1,q}\).}
\item
  \emph{If \(X\sim F_{p,q}\), then
  \[\frac{(p/q)X}{1+(p/q)X}\sim \operatorname{Beta}\left(\frac p2,\frac q2\right).\]}
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 28} (Expected variance ratio). Let
\[F=\frac{S_X^2/\sigma_X^2}{S_Y^2/\sigma_Y^2}\sim F_{n-1,m-1}.\] Assume
\(m>3\). Find \(\mathbb{E}[F]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Write \[F=\frac{\chi^2_{n-1}/(n-1)}{\chi^2_{m-1}/(m-1)},\] where the
numerator and denominator are independent. Since
\[\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\chi^2_{n-1}}{n-1}\right]=1\] and, for
\(m-1>2\),
\[\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{m-1}{\chi^2_{m-1}}\right]=\frac{m-1}{m-3},\] we
get \[\mathbb{E}[F]=\frac{m-1}{m-3}.\] For large \(m\),
\[\mathbb{E}[F]=\frac{m-1}{m-3}\approx 1.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 29} (\(t\) and \(F\)). If \(T\sim t_{12}\),
what is the distribution of \(T^2\)?

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By the relationship between \(t\) and \(F\) distributions,
\[T^2\sim F_{1,12}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Order Statistics}\label{order-statistics}

This section studies the sorted values of a random sample, which are
used to describe extremes, quantiles, ranges, and medians.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 30} (Order statistics). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a
random sample. The \textbf{order statistics} are the ordered values
\[X_{(1)}<X_{(2)}<\cdots<X_{(n)},\] where \(X_{(j)}\) is the \(j\)-th
smallest value among \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\). In particular,
\[X_{(1)}=\min{X_1,\ldots,X_n},
\qquad
X_{(n)}=\max{X_1,\ldots,X_n}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

If ties are possible, as in discrete distributions, one may write
\[X_{(1)}\leq X_{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq X_{(n)}.\] For continuous
distributions, ties have probability zero, so strict ordering is usually
safe.

\subsection{Discrete order statistics}\label{discrete-order-statistics}

This subsection gives the distribution of an order statistic when the
population is discrete.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 31} (Discrete order statistics). \emph{Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from a discrete distribution with
pmf \[f_X(x_i)=p_i,
\qquad x_1<x_2<\cdots.\] Define \[P_0=0,
\qquad
P_i=p_1+\cdots+p_i.\] Then
\[\mathbb{P}(X_{(j)}\leq x_i)=\sum_{k=j}^n {n\choose k}P_i^k(1-P_i)^{n-k},\]
and \[\mathbb{P}(X_{(j)}=x_i)
=\sum_{k=j}^n {n\choose k}
\left[P_i^k(1-P_i)^{n-k}-P_{i-1}^k(1-P_{i-1})^{n-k}\right].\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} The event \({X_{(j)}\leq x_i}\) occurs exactly when at
least \(j\) of the \(n\) observations are less than or equal to \(x_i\).
Each observation has probability \(P_i\) of being less than or equal to
\(x_i\). Therefore the number of observations less than or equal to
\(x_i\) is \(\operatorname{Binomial}(n,P_i)\), giving
\[\mathbb{P}(X_{(j)}\leq x_i)=\sum_{k=j}^n {n\choose k}P_i^k(1-P_i)^{n-k}.\]
Then \[\mathbb{P}(X_{(j)}=x_i)
=\mathbb{P}(X_{(j)}\leq x_i)-\mathbb{P}(X_{(j)}\leq x_{i-1}),\] which
gives the stated formula.~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 32} (Median of three fair die rolls). Roll a fair
six-sided die three times. Let \(X_{(2)}\) be the sample median. Find
\(\mathbb{P}(X_{(2)}\leq 4)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For a fair die, \[P_4=\mathbb{P}(X\leq 4)=\frac46=\frac23.\] The event
\(X_{(2)}\leq4\) means at least two of the three observations are at
most \(4\). Hence \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_{(2)}\leq4)
&={3\choose2}\left(\frac23\right)^2\left(\frac13\right)
+{3\choose3}\left(\frac23\right)^3\\
&=3\cdot\frac49\cdot\frac13+\frac8{27}
=\frac{12}{27}+\frac{8}{27}
=\frac{20}{27}.
\end{aligned}\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Continuous order
statistics}\label{continuous-order-statistics}

This subsection gives the density formulas for continuous order
statistics.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 33} (Pdf of a continuous order statistic). \emph{Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from a continuous population with
cdf \(F_X(x)\) and pdf \(f_X(x)\). Then the pdf of \(X_{(j)}\) is
\[f_{X_{(j)}}(x)
=\frac{n!}{(j-1)!(n-j)!}
 f_X(x)[F_X(x)]^{j-1}[1-F_X(x)]^{n-j}.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} For \(X_{(j)}\) to fall in a small interval near \(x\),
one observation must fall near \(x\), exactly \(j-1\) observations must
be below \(x\), and \(n-j\) observations must be above \(x\). The
combinatorial factor counts which observations play these roles:
\[\frac{n!}{(j-1)!1!(n-j)!}.\] The probability contribution is
approximately \[[F_X(x)]^{j-1} f_X(x)\,dx [1-F_X(x)]^{n-j}.\] Dividing
by \(dx\) gives the density.~◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 34} (Joint pdf of two continuous order statistics).
\emph{Let \(1\leq i<j\leq n\). The joint pdf of \(X_{(i)}\) and
\(X_{(j)}\) is, for \(u<v\), \[\begin{aligned}
f_{X_{(i)},X_{(j)}}(u,v)
&=\frac{n!}{(i-1)!(j-1-i)!(n-j)!}
 f_X(u)f_X(v)[F_X(u)]^{i-1}\\
&\qquad \times [F_X(v)-F_X(u)]^{j-1-i}[1-F_X(v)]^{n-j}.
\end{aligned}\] It is \(0\) otherwise.}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 35} (Joint pdf of all continuous order statistics).
\emph{The joint pdf of \(X_{(1)},X_{(2)},\ldots,X_{(n)}\) is
\[f_{X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=
\begin{cases}
n! f_X(x_1)\cdots f_X(x_n), & -\infty<x_1<\cdots<x_n<\infty,\\
0, &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 36} (Uniform order statistic). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be
a random sample from \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Find the
distribution of \(X_{(j)}\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), \[f_X(x)=1,
\qquad
F_X(x)=x,
\qquad 0<x<1.\] Thus \[f_{X_{(j)}}(x)
=\frac{n!}{(j-1)!(n-j)!}x^{j-1}(1-x)^{n-j},
\qquad 0<x<1.\] This is the beta density with parameters \(j\) and
\(n-j+1\). Therefore \[X_{(j)}\sim \operatorname{Beta}(j,n-j+1).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 37} (Maximum of uniforms). Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).
Find the cdf and pdf of \(X_{(n)}=\max{X_1,\ldots,X_n}\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(0<x<1\),
\[F_{X_{(n)}}(x)=\mathbb{P}(X_{(n)}\leq x)=\mathbb{P}(X_1\leq x,\ldots,X_n\leq x)=x^n.\]
Therefore \[f_{X_{(n)}}(x)=nx^{n-1},\qquad 0<x<1.\] This agrees with
\(\operatorname{Beta}(n,1)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Sample range and median}\label{sample-range-and-median}

This subsection introduces range, median, and quartiles as statistics
built from order statistics.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 38} (Sample range). The \textbf{sample range} is
\[R=X_{(n)}-X_{(1)}.\] It measures the distance between the smallest and
largest observations.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 39} (Sample median and quartiles). The \textbf{sample
median} is a number \(M\) such that approximately one-half of the
observations are below \(M\) and one-half are above \(M\). The lower
quartile is the 25th percentile, and the upper quartile is the 75th
percentile.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 40} (Range from a uniform sample). Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from
\(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,a)\). Find the distribution of the sample
range \[R=X_{(n)}-X_{(1)}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The joint pdf of the minimum and maximum is
\[f_{X_{(1)},X_{(n)}}(x_1,x_n)
=\frac{n(n-1)}{a^n}(x_n-x_1)^{n-2},
\qquad 0<x_1<x_n<a.\] Define \[V=\frac{X_{(n)}+X_{(1)}}{2},
\qquad
R=X_{(n)}-X_{(1)}.\] Then \[X_{(1)}=V-\frac{R}{2},
\qquad
X_{(n)}=V+\frac{R}{2}.\] The absolute value of the Jacobian is \(1\).
The support is \[0<r<a,
\qquad
\frac r2<v<a-\frac r2.\] Thus \[f_{R,V}(r,v)=\frac{n(n-1)r^{n-2}}{a^n},
\qquad 0<r<a,\quad \frac r2<v<a-\frac r2.\] Integrating out \(v\) gives
\[\begin{aligned}
f_R(r)
&=\int_{r/2}^{a-r/2}\frac{n(n-1)r^{n-2}}{a^n}\,dv\\
&=\frac{n(n-1)r^{n-2}(a-r)}{a^n},
\qquad 0<r<a.
\end{aligned}\] If \(a=1\), then \[R\sim \operatorname{Beta}(n-1,2).\]
For arbitrary \(a\), \[\frac{R}{a}\sim \operatorname{Beta}(n-1,2).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 41} (Expected range from uniforms). Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).
Use the distribution of \(R\) to compute \(\mathbb{E}[R]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(a=1\), \[f_R(r)=n(n-1)r^{n-2}(1-r),
\qquad 0<r<1.\] Therefore \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[R]
&=\int_0^1 r\,n(n-1)r^{n-2}(1-r)\,dr\\
&=n(n-1)\int_0^1 (r^{n-1}-r^n)\,dr\\
&=n(n-1)\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right)\\
&=\frac{n-1}{n+1}.
\end{aligned}\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Summary}\label{summary-4}

This section summarizes the main formulas and ideas from sampling and
order statistics.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key formulas}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For a random sample \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance
\(\sigma^2\), \[\mathbb{E}[\overline X]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\overline X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[S^2]=\sigma^2.\] If the sample is normal,
\[\overline X\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
\qquad
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_{n-1},
\qquad
\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.\] For continuous order
statistics, \[f_{X_{(j)}}(x)
=\frac{n!}{(j-1)!(n-j)!}f_X(x)[F_X(x)]^{j-1}[1-F_X(x)]^{n-j}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Conceptual summary}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Random samples are iid random variables from a population
  distribution.
\item
  Statistics are functions of the random sample.
\item
  The sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies from sample
  to sample.
\item
  Normal samples produce especially simple and important sampling
  distributions.
\item
  Order statistics describe sorted data and are used for medians,
  quantiles, minima, maxima, and ranges.
\end{itemize}

\end{tcolorbox}
