\chapter{Chapter 9: Convergence Theory and Limit
Theorems}\label{chapter-9-convergence-theory-and-limit-theorems}

This chapter develops the mathematical language for describing the
limiting behavior of random variables, sample averages, and estimators.
It connects convergence modes with the weak law of large numbers, the
strong law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, continuous
mapping, Slutsky's theorem, and concentration inequalities.

\textbf{Topics.} Convergence of numbers and functions; sequences of
random variables; convergence in distribution, probability, mean, and
almost surely; relationships among modes of convergence; weak and strong
laws of large numbers; central limit theorem; continuous mapping
theorem; Slutsky's theorem; concentration inequalities and
high-dimensional proportion estimation.

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Overview}\label{overview-6}

This section develops the language needed to describe limiting behavior
of random variables, sample averages, and estimators.

In deterministic calculus, a sequence of numbers may converge to a fixed
limit. In probability and statistics, the objects that converge are
often random variables. Since random variables are functions on an
underlying sample space, there are several useful ways for a sequence of
random variables to converge: by the shape of the distribution, by
probability of large deviation, by average error, or by
almost-everywhere sample-path behavior.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The main question is not only whether \(X_n\) approaches \(X\), but also
\emph{in what sense} it approaches \(X\): \[X_n \xrightarrow{D} X,\qquad
X_n \xrightarrow{P} X,\qquad
X_n \xrightarrow{L^r} X,\qquad
X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X.\] These four arrows encode different
mathematical meanings and are used for different statistical purposes.

\end{tcolorbox}

The major results in this section are the weak law of large numbers, the
strong law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, the continuous
mapping theorem, Slutsky's theorem, and concentration inequalities.

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Convergence of Numbers and
Functions}\label{convergence-of-numbers-and-functions}

This section reviews ordinary deterministic convergence before
introducing convergence of random variables.

\section{Convergence of a sequence of
numbers}\label{convergence-of-a-sequence-of-numbers}

A sequence of numbers converges when, eventually, all terms remain
arbitrarily close to a fixed limiting value.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 1} (Convergence of a numerical sequence). A sequence
of numbers \(a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots\) converges to a limit \(a\) if
\[\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n=a.\] More precisely, for every \(\epsilon>0\),
there exists \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) such that
\[|a_n-a|<\epsilon \qquad \text{for all } n>N.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 2} (A basic convergent sequence). Let
\[a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}.\] Show that \(a_n\to 1\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

We have
\[\left|\frac{n}{n+1}-1\right|=\left|\frac{n-(n+1)}{n+1}\right|=\frac{1}{n+1}.\]
Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose \(N>1/\epsilon-1\). Then for all \(n>N\),
\[\frac{1}{n+1}<\epsilon.\] Therefore \(a_n\to 1\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Epsilon-delta definition of a
limit}\label{epsilon-delta-definition-of-a-limit}

The epsilon-delta definition is the formal way to state that the values
of a function become close to a limit when the input becomes close to a
point.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 3} (Limit of a function). We say
\[\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L\] if for every \(\epsilon>0\), there exists
\(\delta>0\) such that whenever \[0<|x-a|<\delta,\] it follows that
\[|f(x)-L|<\epsilon.\] Here \(\epsilon\) measures how close \(f(x)\)
must be to \(L\), and \(\delta\) measures how close \(x\) must be to
\(a\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 4}. The same idea appears repeatedly in probability. In
convergence in probability, for example, the tolerance \(\epsilon\)
controls how far \(X_n\) can be from \(X\), and the probability of
violating that tolerance must go to zero.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 5} (A quick limit check). Use the epsilon-delta
idea to show that \(f(x)=2x+1\) satisfies \[\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=7.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

We compute \[|f(x)-7|=|2x+1-7|=2|x-3|.\] Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose
\(\delta=\epsilon/2\). If \(0<|x-3|<\delta\), then
\[|f(x)-7|=2|x-3|<2\delta=\epsilon.\] Therefore
\(\lim_{x\to 3}(2x+1)=7\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Sequences of Random
Variables}\label{sequences-of-random-variables}

This section explains why convergence of random variables is richer than
convergence of numbers.

Recall that a random variable is a function \[X:S\to \mathbb{R}\] from a
sample space \(S\) to the real numbers. If \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_k\}\) is
finite, then a random variable is determined by its values
\[X(s_i)=x_i,\qquad i=1,
\ldots,k.\] A sequence of random variables \[X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots\] is
therefore a sequence of functions \[X_n:S\to \mathbb{R}.\] For each
outcome \(s\in S\), the sequence \(X_1(s),X_2(s),\ldots\) is an ordinary
sequence of numbers. But random variables also have distributions,
probabilities, expectations, and variances. This creates several
different modes of convergence.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 6} (A sequence of random variables on a finite sample
space). Let \(S=\{s_1,s_2\}\) with
\(\mathbb{P}(s_1)=\mathbb{P}(s_2)=1/2\), and define
\[X_n(s_1)=\frac{1}{n},\qquad X_n(s_2)=1+\frac{1}{n}.\] Find the
pointwise limit \(X(s)=\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(s)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(s_1\), \[X_n(s_1)=\frac{1}{n}\to 0.\] For \(s_2\),
\[X_n(s_2)=1+\frac{1}{n}\to 1.\] Thus the pointwise limiting random
variable is \[X(s_1)=0,
\qquad
X(s_2)=1.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Convergence in Distribution}\label{convergence-in-distribution}

This section introduces the weakest and most distribution-centered mode
of convergence.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 7} (Convergence in distribution). Let \(X_n\) have
CDF \(F_n\) and let \(X\) have CDF \(F\). We say that \(X_n\)
\textbf{converges in distribution} to \(X\), also called convergence
weakly or convergence in law, if \[\lim_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)=F(x)\] for
every continuity point \(x\) of \(F\). We write
\[X_n \xrightarrow{D} X.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Convergence in distribution means that the overall shape of the
distribution of \(X_n\) converges to the overall shape of the
distribution of \(X\). It does not necessarily mean that \(X_n\) and
\(X\) are close on the same sample space.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 8} (Normal distributions with variances converging to
one). Let \[X_n\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(0,1+\frac{1}{n}\right).\]
Show that \[X_n\xrightarrow{D}\operatorname{Normal}(0,1).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The CDF of \(X_n\) is
\[F_n(x)=\Phi\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+1/n}}\right),\] where \(\Phi\) is
the standard normal CDF. Since \[\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+1/n}}\to x\] and
\(\Phi\) is continuous,
\[F_n(x)=\Phi\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+1/n}}\right)\to \Phi(x).\] Therefore
\(X_n\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{chapters/chapter-09-convergence-theory_files/figure-pdf/fig-normal-convergence-ch9-output-1.pdf}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-normal-convergence-ch9}Densities N(0,2), N(0,1.2),
and N(0,1) illustrating convergence in distribution.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 9} (CDF convergence). Let
\(X_n\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1+1/n)\). Show that
\(X_n\xrightarrow{D}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For \(0<x<1\), \[F_n(x)=\frac{x}{1+1/n}\to x.\] For \(x\le 0\),
\(F_n(x)=0\to 0\). For \(x>1\), eventually \(x>1+1/n\), so
\(F_n(x)=1\to 1\). These are exactly the values of the CDF of
\(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) at its continuity points. Therefore
\(X_n\xrightarrow{D}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Convergence in Probability}\label{convergence-in-probability}

This section introduces the mode of convergence most closely connected
to statistical consistency.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 10} (Convergence in probability). A sequence \(X_n\)
converges in probability to \(X\) if for every \(\epsilon>0\),
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)=0.\] We write
\[X_n\xrightarrow{P}X.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Convergence in probability means that large deviations from the limiting
random variable become rare.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 11} (A shrinking normal sequence). Let
\[X_n\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right).\] Show that
\(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\), and identify the distributional limit of
\(\sqrt nX_n\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For any \(\epsilon>0\), Chebyshev's inequality gives
\[\mathbb{P}(|X_n-0|>\epsilon)
\le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_n)}{\epsilon^2}
=\frac{1}{n\epsilon^2}\to 0.\] Thus \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).

Also, since \(X_n\sim N(0,1/n)\), \[\sqrt n X_n\sim N(0,1).\] Therefore
\[\sqrt nX_n\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1).\] This example shows that a sequence
can converge to \(0\) in probability while a rescaled version has a
non-degenerate limiting distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 12} (Binary sequence converging in probability). Let
\[\mathbb{P}(X_n=0)=1-\frac1n,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X_n=1)=\frac1n.\] Show that \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(0<\epsilon<1\). Then
\[\mathbb{P}(|X_n-0|>\epsilon)=\mathbb{P}(X_n=1)=\frac1n\to 0.\] For
\(\epsilon\ge 1\), the probability is already \(0\). Thus
\(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Convergence in probability implies convergence in
distribution}\label{convergence-in-probability-implies-convergence-in-distribution}

This subsection states a key implication and shows why the converse is
not true in general.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 13} (Convergence in probability implies convergence in
distribution). \emph{If \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\), then
\[X_n\xrightarrow{D}X.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 14} (Same distribution does not imply convergence in
probability). Let \(X\sim N(0,1)\) and define
\[X_n=-X\qquad \text{for all } n.\] Then \(X_n\xrightarrow{D}X\), but
\(X_n\) does not converge in probability to \(X\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(X\) and \(-X\) have the same standard normal distribution, every
\(X_n=-X\) has the same distribution as \(X\). Therefore
\(X_n\xrightarrow{D}X\).

However, \[|X_n-X|=|-X-X|=2|X|.\] Hence
\[\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>1)=\mathbb{P}(2|X|>1)=\mathbb{P}(|X|>1/2),\] which
is a positive constant and does not go to \(0\). Therefore \(X_n\) does
not converge in probability to \(X\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 15} (Distributional convergence to a constant). \emph{If
\(X_n\xrightarrow{D}c\), where \(c\) is a constant, then
\[X_n\xrightarrow{P}c.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 16}. The theorem is special to the case where the limiting
random variable is constant. When the limit is random, convergence in
distribution alone does not imply convergence in probability.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Convergence in Mean}\label{convergence-in-mean}

This section introduces convergence based on the expected size of the
error.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 17} (Convergence in \(r\)-th mean). Let \(r\ge 1\) be
fixed. We say that \(X_n\) converges in the \(r\)-th mean to \(X\) if
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|^r=0.\] We write
\[X_n\xrightarrow{L^r}X.\] The case \(r=1\) is convergence in mean, and
the case \(r=2\) is convergence in mean square.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 18} (Uniform sequence converging in \(L^r\)). Let
\[X_n\sim \operatorname{Uniform}\left(0,\frac1n\right).\] Show that
\(X_n\xrightarrow{L^r}0\) for every fixed \(r\ge 1\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The density of \(X_n\) is \(n\) on \((0,1/n)\). Thus
\[\mathbb{E}|X_n-0|^r
=\int_0^{1/n} x^r n\,dx
= n\cdot \frac{(1/n)^{r+1}}{r+1}
=\frac{1}{(r+1)n^r}\to 0.\] Therefore \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^r}0\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Mean convergence implies probability
convergence}\label{mean-convergence-implies-probability-convergence}

This subsection uses Markov's inequality to connect convergence in mean
with convergence in probability.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 19} (\(L^r\) convergence implies convergence in
probability). \emph{If \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^r}X\) for some \(r\ge 1\),
then \[X_n\xrightarrow{P}X.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} For any \(\epsilon>0\), Markov's inequality applied to
\(|X_n-X|^r\) gives \[\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)
=\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|^r>\epsilon^r)
\le \frac{\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|^r}{\epsilon^r}.\] If
\(\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|^r\to 0\), then the right-hand side goes to \(0\).
Hence \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\). ◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 20} (Convergence in probability without convergence in
mean). Define \(X_n\) by \[\mathbb{P}(X_n=0)=1-\frac1n,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X_n=n^2)=\frac1n.\] Show that \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\) but
\(\mathbb{E}X_n\to\infty\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For any fixed \(\epsilon>0\), once \(n^2>\epsilon\),
\[\mathbb{P}(|X_n-0|>\epsilon)=\mathbb{P}(X_n=n^2)=\frac1n\to 0.\] Thus
\(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).

However,
\[\mathbb{E}X_n=0\left(1-\frac1n\right)+n^2\cdot \frac1n=n\to\infty.\]
Therefore convergence in probability does not imply convergence in mean.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Almost Sure Convergence}\label{almost-sure-convergence}

This section gives the strongest sample-path mode of convergence used in
this course.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 21} (Almost sure convergence). The sequence \(X_n\)
converges almost surely to \(X\) if
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n=X\right)=1.\] Equivalently,
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\omega:\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\right)=1.\]
We write \[X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Interpretation Almost sure convergence means that, with probability
\(1\), the actual sample path \(X_n(\omega)\) converges pointwise to
\(X(\omega)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 22} (Almost sure convergence implies convergence in
probability). \emph{If \(X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X\), then
\[X_n\xrightarrow{P}X.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Reason.} Almost sure convergence says that for almost every
\(\omega\), the numerical sequence \(X_n(\omega)\) converges to
\(X(\omega)\). Therefore, for any \(\epsilon>0\), the event
\[A_{n,\epsilon}=\{\omega: |X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\epsilon\}\] must
eventually become rare. This implies
\[\mathbb{P}(A_{n,\epsilon})\to 0,\] which is precisely convergence in
probability. ◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\includegraphics[width=5.83in,height=2.9in]{chapters/chapter-09-convergence-theory_files/figure-latex/mermaid-figure-1.png}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Common mistake}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Common mistake The arrows above are one-way in general. For example,
convergence in distribution does not usually imply convergence in
probability, and convergence in probability does not usually imply
convergence in mean.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 23} (Identifying modes of convergence). Suppose
\(X_n=Z/n\), where \(Z\) is a random variable with
\(\mathbb{E}Z^2<\infty\). Show that \(X_n\to 0\) almost surely and in
\(L^2\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For every outcome \(\omega\) such that \(Z(\omega)\) is finite,
\[X_n(\omega)=\frac{Z(\omega)}{n}\to 0.\] Since \(Z\) is finite almost
surely, \(X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}0\).

Also,
\[\mathbb{E}|X_n|^2=\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\right)=\frac{\mathbb{E}Z^2}{n^2}\to 0.\]
Therefore \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^2}0\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Weak Law of Large Numbers}\label{weak-law-of-large-numbers}

This section states and proves the law saying that sample averages
converge to the population mean in probability.

Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be iid random variables from a distribution
\(F\). The sample average is \[\overline X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 24} (Weak law of large numbers). \emph{Suppose
\(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) are iid with mean \[\mu=\mathbb{E}X_i<\infty\] and
finite variance \[\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty.\] Then
\[\overline X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu.\] That is, for every \(\epsilon>0\),
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-\mu|>\epsilon)=0.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} We know \[\mathbb{E}\overline X_n=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.\] By Chebyshev's
inequality, \[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-\mu|\ge \epsilon)
\le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)}{\epsilon^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}\to 0.\] Therefore
\(\overline X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu\). ◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 25} (Coin flips). Let
\(X_i\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) be iid, where \(X_i=1\) means
heads and \(X_i=0\) means tails. Let
\[\overline X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.\] Interpret the weak law of
large numbers.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here \(\mathbb{E}X_i=p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=p(1-p)\). The
WLLN gives \[\overline X_n\xrightarrow{P}p.\] The sample proportion of
heads converges in probability to the true probability of heads.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Strong Law of Large Numbers}\label{strong-law-of-large-numbers}

This section states the stronger sample-path version of the law of large
numbers.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 26} (Strong law of large numbers). \emph{Suppose
\(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) are iid with finite mean \[\mu=\mathbb{E}X_i<\infty\]
and finite variance \[\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty.\] Then
\[\overline X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu.\] Equivalently,
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\overline X_n=\mu\right)=1.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 27}. The weak law says the probability of a large error
goes to \(0\). The strong law says that, with probability \(1\), the
sequence of observed sample averages itself converges to \(\mu\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 28} (Long-run frequency). In repeated iid Bernoulli
trials with success probability \(p\), the sample proportion of
successes satisfies \[\overline X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}p.\] This
formalizes the long-run frequency interpretation of probability.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(X_i\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) have finite mean \(p\) and
finite variance \(p(1-p)\), the strong law applies directly:
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\overline X_n=p\right)=1.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Central Limit Theorem}\label{central-limit-theorem}

This section states the central approximation result explaining why
normal distributions appear throughout statistics.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 29} (Central limit theorem). \emph{Suppose
\(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) are iid with mean \[\mu=\mathbb{E}X_i<\infty\] and
variance \[\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty.\] Then
\[\frac{\overline X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1).\]
Equivalently,
\[\overline X_n \approx N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\] for large
\(n\), and \[X_1+\cdots+X_n \approx N(n\mu,n\sigma^2).\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Common mistake}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Precise interpretation The expression
\[\overline X_n \approx N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\] is an
approximation for large \(n\). The exact convergence statement is the
standardized convergence
\[\frac{\overline X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 30} (Binomial approximation). Let
\(X\sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\). Use the CLT to approximate the
distribution of \(X\) for large \(n\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Write \[X=X_1+\cdots+X_n,\] where
\(X_i\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) are iid. Then \(\mu=p\) and
\(\sigma^2=p(1-p)\). By the CLT,
\[\frac{X-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1).\] Thus for large
\(n\), \[X\approx N(np,np(1-p)).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 31} (Standardized sample mean). Suppose
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are iid with \(\mathbb{E}X_i=10\) and
\(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=25\). Find the approximate distribution of
\(\overline X_n\) for large \(n\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here \(\mu=10\) and \(\sigma^2=25\). The CLT gives
\[\frac{\overline X_n-10}{5/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1),\] so for
large \(n\), \[\overline X_n\approx N\left(10,\frac{25}{n}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Continuous Mapping and Slutsky's
Theorem}\label{continuous-mapping-and-slutskys-theorem}

This section gives two tools for transforming convergent random
variables.

\section{Continuous mapping theorem}\label{continuous-mapping-theorem}

The continuous mapping theorem says that continuous transformations
preserve convergence.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 32} (Continuous mapping theorem). \emph{Let \(g\) be a
continuous function.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \emph{If \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\), then \[g(X_n)\xrightarrow{P}g(X).\]}
\item
  \emph{If \(X_n\xrightarrow{D}X\), then \[g(X_n)\xrightarrow{D}g(X).\]}
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 33} (Squaring a consistent estimator). Suppose
\(X_n\xrightarrow{P}\theta\). Show that
\(X_n^2\xrightarrow{P}\theta^2\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Use the continuous mapping theorem with \(g(x)=x^2\), which is
continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\). Therefore
\[X_n^2=g(X_n)\xrightarrow{P}g(\theta)=\theta^2.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Slutsky's theorem}\label{slutskys-theorem}

Slutsky's theorem is essential for asymptotic statistics because it lets
us replace unknown constants by consistent estimates.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 34} (Slutsky's theorem). \emph{If \[X_n\xrightarrow{D}X
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
Y_n\xrightarrow{P}c,\] where \(c\) is a constant, then
\[X_n+Y_n\xrightarrow{D}X+c,\] \[X_nY_n\xrightarrow{D}cX,\] and if
\(c\ne 0\), \[\frac{X_n}{Y_n}\xrightarrow{D}\frac{X}{c}.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 35} (Replacing variance by a consistent estimator).
Suppose
\[\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1)\] and
suppose \(S_n\xrightarrow{P}\sigma\), with \(\sigma>0\). Show that
\[\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{S_n}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Write \[\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{S_n}
=\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\cdot \frac{\sigma}{S_n}.\]
The first factor converges in distribution to \(N(0,1)\). Since
\(S_n\xrightarrow{P}\sigma\), the second factor satisfies
\[\frac{\sigma}{S_n}\xrightarrow{P}1.\] By Slutsky's theorem, the
product converges in distribution to \[N(0,1)\cdot 1=N(0,1).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Statistical Meaning of
Convergence}\label{statistical-meaning-of-convergence}

This section connects convergence theory to estimation and inference.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  Convergence in probability is related to \textbf{statistical
  consistency}. An estimator \(\widehat\theta_n\) is consistent for
  \(\theta\) if \[\widehat\theta_n\xrightarrow{P}\theta.\]
\item
  Convergence in distribution is often used to construct maximum
  likelihood approximations, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests.
\item
  The CLT often provides the limiting distribution of a properly
  standardized estimator.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 36} (Sample mean as a consistent estimator). Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be iid with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance. Show
that \(\overline X_n\) is a consistent estimator of \(\mu\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By the weak law of large numbers, \[\overline X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu.\]
Therefore \(\overline X_n\) is consistent for \(\mu\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Concentration Inequalities and
Rates}\label{concentration-inequalities-and-rates}

This section explains how concentration inequalities strengthen
convergence statements by providing explicit finite-sample bounds.

A concentration inequality aims to find a function
\(\phi_n(\epsilon)\to 0\) such that
\[\mathbb{P}(|X_n-\mathbb{E}X_n|>\epsilon)\le \phi_n(\epsilon).\] This
automatically gives convergence in probability. The rate at which
\(\phi_n(\epsilon)\) goes to zero describes how fast \(X_n\)
concentrates around its expectation.

\section{Concentration of a Gaussian
mean}\label{concentration-of-a-gaussian-mean}

This subsection derives a Gaussian-rate tail bound for the sample mean
of normal observations.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 37} (Gaussian sample mean concentration). Let
\[X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\] and let
\(\overline X_n\) be the sample mean. Show that
\[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n|>\epsilon)
\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(X_i\) are normal,
\[\overline X_n\sim N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).\] Let
\(Z\sim N(0,1)\). Then \[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n|>\epsilon)
=\mathbb{P}\left(|Z|>\frac{\sqrt n\epsilon}{\sigma}\right).\] Using the
standard normal tail bound \[\mathbb{P}(|Z|>t)\le 2e^{-t^2/2},\] we
obtain \[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n|>\epsilon)
\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Concentration of a maximum}\label{concentration-of-a-maximum}

This subsection shows how a union bound converts a one-variable tail
bound into a maximum tail bound.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 38} (Maximum of Gaussian variables). Let
\[X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2)\] and define
\[Z_n=\max\{|X_1|,\ldots,|X_n|\}.\] Show that \[\mathbb{P}(Z_n>\epsilon)
\le 2n\exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By the union bound, \[\mathbb{P}(Z_n>\epsilon)
=\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n\{|X_i|>\epsilon\}\right)
\le \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}(|X_i|>\epsilon).\] For each \(i\),
\[\mathbb{P}(|X_i|>\epsilon)
\le 2\exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\] Therefore
\[\mathbb{P}(Z_n>\epsilon)
\le 2n\exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Chebyshev versus Hoeffding for sample
means}\label{chebyshev-versus-hoeffding-for-sample-means}

This subsection compares polynomial and exponential rates for the sample
mean.

Recall Chebyshev's inequality: \[\mathbb{P}(|X-\mathbb{E}X|\ge \epsilon)
\le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\epsilon^2}.\] If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\)
are iid with variance \(\sigma^2\), then
\[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-\mathbb{E}\overline X_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le \frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}.\] This gives a rate of order \(1/n\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 39} (Hoeffding's inequality). \emph{Suppose \(X_1,
\ldots,X_n\) are independent and \(0\le X_i\le 1\). Then for any
\(\epsilon>0\),
\[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-\mathbb{E}\overline X_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le 2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.\] More generally, if \(a\le X_i\le b\), then the
result can be scaled accordingly.}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 40}. Hoeffding's inequality gives exponential
concentration. This is much faster than the rate given by Chebyshev's
inequality. Such exponential rates are important in high-dimensional
statistics, nonparametric inference, semiparametric inference, and
empirical risk minimization.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 41} (Comparing bounds). Suppose
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\)
and \(\overline X_n\) is the sample proportion. Give a Chebyshev bound
and a Hoeffding bound for \[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-p|\ge \epsilon).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Since \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=p(1-p)\), Chebyshev gives
\[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-p|\ge \epsilon)
\le \frac{p(1-p)}{n\epsilon^2}.\] Since Bernoulli variables lie in
\([0,1]\), Hoeffding gives \[\mathbb{P}(|\overline X_n-p|\ge \epsilon)
\le 2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.\] The Hoeffding bound decays exponentially in
\(n\), while the Chebyshev bound decays only like \(1/n\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Consistency of estimating a high-dimensional
proportion}\label{consistency-of-estimating-a-high-dimensional-proportion}

This subsection illustrates why concentration inequalities are central
in modern statistics.

Consider iid binary observations \[X_1,
\ldots,X_n\in \{0,1\}^d.\] Write \[X_i=(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{id}),\] and
suppose \[\mathbb{E}X_{ij}=p_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,d.\] The sample proportion estimator for coordinate
\(j\) is \[\widehat p_j=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}.\] We want all \(d\)
coordinates to be close to their targets simultaneously:
\[\max_{1\le j\le d}|\widehat p_j-p_j|.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 42} (Uniform concentration for binary proportions).
\emph{For any \(\epsilon>0\),
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{1\le j\le d}|\widehat p_j-p_j|\ge \epsilon\right)
\le 2d e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Proof}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Proof.} For a fixed coordinate \(j\), Hoeffding's inequality gives
\[\mathbb{P}(|\widehat p_j-p_j|\ge \epsilon)
\le 2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.\] Using the union bound over \(j=1,
\ldots,d\),
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{1\le j\le d}|\widehat p_j-p_j|\ge \epsilon\right)
=\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^d\{|
\widehat p_j-p_j|\ge \epsilon\}\right)
\le \sum_{j=1}^d 2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.\] Therefore
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{1\le j\le d}|\widehat p_j-p_j|\ge \epsilon\right)
\le 2d e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.\] ◻

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The bound \[2d e^{-2n\epsilon^2}\] shows that the sample size \(n\) must
grow at least on the order of \(\log d\) to control all \(d\)
coordinates simultaneously. This logarithmic dependence on dimension is
a key theme in high-dimensional probability and statistics.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 43} (Sample size from a concentration bound).
Find a sufficient sample size \(n\) so that
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{1\le j\le d}|\widehat p_j-p_j|\ge \epsilon\right)
\le \alpha.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

It is enough to require \[2d e^{-2n\epsilon^2}\le \alpha.\] Taking
logarithms, \[\log(2d)-2n\epsilon^2\le \log\alpha.\] Equivalently,
\[2n\epsilon^2\ge \log\left(\frac{2d}{\alpha}\right).\] Thus a
sufficient condition is
\[n\ge \frac{1}{2\epsilon^2}\log\left(\frac{2d}{\alpha}\right).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Summary of Modes of
Convergence}\label{summary-of-modes-of-convergence}

This section summarizes the four modes of convergence and their main
relationships.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}

Mode

\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Distribution & \(F_n(x)\to F(x)\) at continuity points of \(F\) &
Distributional shape converges \\
Probability & \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)\to 0\) & Large errors
become rare \\
\(r\)-th mean & \(\mathbb{E}|X_n-X|^r\to 0\) & Average \(r\)-th power
error vanishes \\
Almost surely & \(\mathbb{P}(\lim X_n=X)=1\) & Sample paths converge
with probability \(1\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\[X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X \Longrightarrow X_n\xrightarrow{P}X \Longrightarrow X_n\xrightarrow{D}X.\]
Also, \[X_n\xrightarrow{L^r}X \Longrightarrow X_n\xrightarrow{P}X.\] The
converses are generally false without additional assumptions.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 44} (Choosing the right theorem). For each
goal, identify the most relevant theorem.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Show that a sample mean is close to \(\mu\) for large \(n\).
\item
  Approximate the distribution of a standardized sample mean.
\item
  Replace an unknown \(\sigma\) by a consistent estimator \(S_n\) in an
  asymptotic normal statement.
\item
  Show that \(g(\widehat\theta_n)\) is consistent if
  \(\widehat\theta_n\) is consistent.
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Use the weak law of large numbers, or a concentration inequality if a
  finite-sample rate is needed.
\item
  Use the central limit theorem.
\item
  Use Slutsky's theorem.
\item
  Use the continuous mapping theorem.
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}
