\chapter{Chapter 10: Monte Carlo
Sampling}\label{chapter-10-monte-carlo-sampling}

This chapter introduces Monte Carlo methods as a practical bridge
between probability theory, statistical inference, numerical
integration, simulation, Bayesian computation, and optimization. The
main principle is to rewrite a difficult quantity as a probability or
expectation, simulate random samples, and approximate the target with a
sample average.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Topics}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Introduction and applications; simulation; Monte Carlo integration; Law
of Large Numbers foundation; standard random-number generation;
inverse-transform sampling; Box--Muller normal sampling; rejection
sampling; importance sampling; sampling-importance-resampling;
advantages and limitations.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Overview}\label{overview-7}

This section introduces Monte Carlo methods as a systematic way to use
randomness to approximate quantities that are difficult to compute
exactly.

Monte Carlo methods are algorithms that approximate numerical answers by
repeated random sampling. The key idea is simple: if a quantity can be
written as an expectation or probability, then it can often be
approximated by an average over simulated random samples.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Main message Monte Carlo sampling replaces a difficult probability,
expectation, integral, sum, or optimization problem by a random
experiment that can be repeated many times:
\[\text{target quantity} \approx \text{sample average from simulated draws}.\]
The accuracy improves as the number of samples increases, by the Law of
Large Numbers.

\end{tcolorbox}

This section emphasizes four central ideas:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  using simulation to estimate averages and probabilities;
\item
  using Monte Carlo integration to approximate integrals;
\item
  generating random variables from desired distributions;
\item
  using rejection sampling and importance sampling when direct sampling
  is hard.
\end{enumerate}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Background and History}\label{background-and-history}

This section places Monte Carlo sampling in its historical and
conceptual context.

\section{Historical background}\label{historical-background}

Monte Carlo methods are named after Monte Carlo, the famous casino
district in Monaco. The name reflects the central role of chance in
these methods, much like chance drives games of roulette.

Historically, several ideas contributed to Monte Carlo methods:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Buffon's needle problem} was studied by Georges-Louis Leclerc,
  Comte de Buffon, in the eighteenth century and gave an early example
  of using random experiments to estimate \(\pi\).
\item
  \textbf{Markov chains} were introduced by Andrey Markov to describe
  systems whose future evolution depends on the present state rather
  than the full past.
\item
  \textbf{Ulam and von Neumann} used Monte Carlo methods in the 1940s
  during the Manhattan Project, for example in neutron diffusion
  simulations.
\item
  \textbf{Markov chain Monte Carlo} later developed through algorithms
  such as Metropolis--Hastings, Gibbs sampling, and Hamiltonian Monte
  Carlo.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Historical timeline

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Markov models and Monte Carlo
sampling}\label{markov-models-and-monte-carlo-sampling}

A Markov model describes a system that evolves over time according to a
memoryless rule.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 1} (Markov chain). A Markov chain is a sequence of
random states in which the probability of the next state depends only on
the current state, not on the full history.

\end{tcolorbox}

Monte Carlo sampling is broader than Markov chains. It refers to methods
that sample from probability distributions in order to estimate desired
quantities. Markov chain Monte Carlo, or MCMC, is used when direct
independent sampling is difficult, but constructing a Markov chain with
the desired stationary distribution is possible.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 2}. Monte Carlo sampling has limitations when the target
distribution is high-dimensional, sharply concentrated, multimodal, or
known only up to a normalizing constant. These limitations motivate
rejection sampling, importance sampling, and MCMC.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{How Monte Carlo Works}\label{how-monte-carlo-works}

This section explains the basic Monte Carlo principle: repeated random
sampling produces numerical approximations.

\section{The basic Monte Carlo idea}\label{the-basic-monte-carlo-idea}

Monte Carlo methods use random sampling and statistical modeling to
estimate mathematical functions or mimic complex systems.

A typical Monte Carlo procedure has the following form:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Choose a probability model for the uncertain quantities.
\item
  Generate random samples from that probability model.
\item
  Evaluate the quantity of interest for each sample.
\item
  Average the results.
\item
  Use more samples to improve accuracy.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Monte Carlo principle If
\(X_1,\ldots,X_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}p(x)\) and \(g\) is a
function, then \[\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int g(x)p(x)\,\,dx\] can be
approximated by \[\widehat{I}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g(X_i).\] By
the Law of Large Numbers,
\[\widehat{I}_N \xrightarrow{P} \mathbb{E}[g(X)].\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Applications}\label{applications}

Monte Carlo methods appear in many areas because many scientific and
statistical questions can be written as expectations, probabilities, or
high-dimensional integrals.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Simulation.} We learn about a random object by generating and
  observing many realizations of it. Examples include risk assessment
  and the spread of disease.
\item
  \textbf{Monte Carlo integration.} We estimate an integral by writing
  it as an expectation of a random variable.
\item
  \textbf{Statistical sampling.} MCMC and related methods are used in
  Bayesian inference, posterior computation, model fitting, and
  parameter estimation.
\item
  \textbf{Optimization.} Random search and simulated annealing use
  random sampling to explore complicated objective functions.
\item
  \textbf{Physical simulation.} Monte Carlo methods are fundamental in
  nuclear physics, statistical mechanics, computer graphics, and
  reinforcement learning.
\end{itemize}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Foundation: Law of Large
Numbers}\label{foundation-law-of-large-numbers}

This section reviews the probabilistic foundation that makes Monte Carlo
possible.

\section{Motivating example: average
height}\label{motivating-example-average-height}

Suppose we want to know the average height of students in a class. If
the class is small, we can measure everyone and compute the ordinary
average.

Now suppose we want to estimate the average height of all people in
Boston. Let \(\mathcal{B}\) denote the population and let \(f(x)\) be
the height of person \(x\). The population average is
\[\mathbb{E}_{x\in\mathcal{B}}[f(x)] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{B}} f(x),\]
which may be infeasible to compute exactly. Instead, we randomly survey
\(S\) people \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(S)}\) and use
\[\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S f(x^{(s)}).\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Simulation summary Use a sample mean to approximate a true mean.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Weak Law of Large Numbers}\label{weak-law-of-large-numbers-1}

The Law of Large Numbers explains why sample averages approximate
expectations.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 3} (Weak Law of Large Numbers). \emph{Let
\(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be IID random variables with common finite mean
\(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Define the sample mean
\[\overline{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}(X_1+\cdots+X_n).\] Then
\[\overline{X}_n \xrightarrow{P} \mu.\] Equivalently, for every
\(\epsilon>0\),
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(|\overline{X}_n-\mu|\ge \epsilon\big)=0.\]}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The proof uses Chebyshev's inequality. Since the \(X_i\) are
independent,
\[\mathbb{E}[\overline{X}_n]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\overline{X}_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.\]
Therefore, \[\mathbb{P}(|\overline{X}_n-\mu|\ge \epsilon)
\le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\overline{X}_n)}{\epsilon^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}\to 0.\] This proves convergence in
probability.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 4} (Monte Carlo convergence rate). For many Monte Carlo
averages, the standard error is proportional to \[\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}},\]
where \(N\) is the number of samples. This convergence is reliable but
may be slow.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{\texorpdfstring{Application I: Simulation and Estimating
\(\pi\)}{Application I: Simulation and Estimating \textbackslash pi}}\label{application-i-simulation-and-estimating-pi}

This section shows how a probability can be estimated by simulating
random points.

\section{Uniform raindrops in a
square}\label{uniform-raindrops-in-a-square}

Suppose raindrops fall uniformly at random over a square \([-1,1]^2\).
Inside the square is the unit circle \[x^2+y^2\le 1.\] The square has
area \(4\), and the circle has area \(\pi\). Therefore, if \(p\) is the
probability that a random point lands in the circle, then
\[p=\frac{\text{area of circle}}{\text{area of square}}=\frac{\pi}{4}.\]
Thus \[\pi = 4p.\]

If we generate random points \((X_i,Y_i)\) uniformly from \([-1,1]^2\),
then
\[\widehat{p}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{1}\{X_i^2+Y_i^2\le 1\}\]
estimates \(p\), so \[\widehat{\pi}_N = 4\widehat{p}_N
=4\frac{\#\{\text{points inside circle}\}}{\#\{\text{points inside square}\}}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 5} (Monte Carlo estimate of \(\pi\)). Use uniformly
sampled points in \([-1,1]^2\) to estimate \(\pi\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \[I_i=\mathbf{1}\{X_i^2+Y_i^2\le 1\}.\] Then
\(I_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) with \(p=\pi/4\). The sample mean
\[\overline{I}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\] converges in probability
to \(p\). Therefore \[4\overline{I}_N \xrightarrow{P} 4p = \pi.\] For
example, using more samples should move the estimate closer to \(\pi\)
on average. Typical simulations may give values such as \(3.2\) for
\(500\) samples, \(3.1312\) for \(10{,}000\) samples, and \(3.142208\)
for \(10^6\) samples.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Python simulation}\label{python-simulation}

The following Python code estimates \(\pi\) by random sampling.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ random}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ estimate\_pi(num\_samples):}
\NormalTok{    inside\_circle }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(num\_samples):}
\NormalTok{        x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ random.uniform(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ random.uniform(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ x}\OperatorTok{**}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ y}\OperatorTok{**}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{\textless{}=} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            inside\_circle }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

    \ControlFlowTok{return} \DecValTok{4} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (inside\_circle }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ num\_samples)}

\NormalTok{num\_samples }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1\_000\_000}
\NormalTok{pi\_estimate }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ estimate\_pi(num\_samples)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Estimated value of pi:"}\NormalTok{, pi\_estimate)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{MATLAB simulation}\label{matlab-simulation}

The same idea can be implemented in MATLAB.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{function} \VariableTok{estimated\_pi} \OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{estimate\_pi}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{num\_samples}\NormalTok{)}
    \VariableTok{inside\_circle} \OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0}\OperatorTok{;}
    \KeywordTok{for} \VariableTok{i} \OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1}\OperatorTok{:}\VariableTok{num\_samples}
        \VariableTok{x} \OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{2}\OperatorTok{*}\VariableTok{rand}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{1}\OperatorTok{;}
        \VariableTok{y} \OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{2}\OperatorTok{*}\VariableTok{rand}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{1}\OperatorTok{;}
        \VariableTok{distance} \OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{x}\OperatorTok{\^{}}\FloatTok{2} \OperatorTok{+} \VariableTok{y}\OperatorTok{\^{}}\FloatTok{2}\OperatorTok{;}
        \KeywordTok{if} \VariableTok{distance} \OperatorTok{\textless{}=} \FloatTok{1}
            \VariableTok{inside\_circle} \OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{inside\_circle} \OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1}\OperatorTok{;}
        \KeywordTok{end}
    \KeywordTok{end}
    \VariableTok{estimated\_pi} \OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{4} \OperatorTok{*} \VariableTok{inside\_circle} \OperatorTok{/} \VariableTok{num\_samples}\OperatorTok{;}
\KeywordTok{end}

\CommentTok{\% Example usage}
\VariableTok{num\_samples} \OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1000000}\OperatorTok{;}
\VariableTok{pi\_estimate} \OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{estimate\_pi}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{num\_samples}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\VariableTok{disp}\NormalTok{([}\SpecialStringTok{\textquotesingle{}Estimated value of pi: \textquotesingle{}}\OperatorTok{,} \VariableTok{num2str}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{pi\_estimate}\NormalTok{)])}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Warning}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Common coding detail If the square is \([-1,1]^2\), use
\(x=2\operatorname{rand}()-1\) and \(y=2\operatorname{rand}()-1\). If
instead \(x,y\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), then the simulation
estimates a quarter circle rather than the full square setup.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Buffon's Needle Problem}\label{buffons-needle-problem}

This section gives a classical Monte Carlo method for estimating \(\pi\)
using random line crossings.

\section{Geometric setup}\label{geometric-setup}

In Buffon's needle problem, parallel lines are separated by distance
\(D\). A needle of length \(L\) is dropped at random, with \(L\le D\).
Let \(P\) be the probability that the needle crosses a line.

If \(\theta\) is the angle between the needle and the lines, and if
\(y\) is the distance from the needle center to the nearest line, then
the needle crosses a line if the vertical projection of half the needle
is at least \(y\): \[y \le \frac{L}{2}\sin\theta.\] The classical
formula is \[P=\frac{2L}{\pi D}.\] Therefore, \[\pi = \frac{2L}{DP}.\]
If \(k\) out of \(n\) dropped needles cross a line, then
\(P\approx k/n\) and \[\widehat{\pi}=\frac{2Ln}{Dk}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 6} (Buffon's needle estimate). Suppose \(L=1\), \(D=2\),
and \(n\) needles are dropped. If \(k\) needles cross a line, estimate
\(\pi\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here \[P=\frac{2L}{\pi D}=\frac{1}{\pi}.\] Since \(P\approx k/n\), we
obtain \[\frac{k}{n}\approx \frac{1}{\pi},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\widehat{\pi}=\frac{n}{k}.\] This estimator is intuitive, but
convergence is slow. Around \(100{,}000\) trials may be needed for only
a few correct digits.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 7}. Buffon's needle is historically important because it
makes the connection between geometry, probability, and numerical
estimation very transparent. It is not computationally efficient
compared with modern numerical methods.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Application II: Monte Carlo
Integration}\label{application-ii-monte-carlo-integration}

This section explains how to approximate integrals by rewriting them as
expectations.

\section{Expectation as integration}\label{expectation-as-integration}

Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with density \(p(x)\). Then
\[\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)p(x)\,\,dx.\] If
\(X_1,\ldots,X_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}p(x)\), then
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)p(x)\,\,dx
\approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g(X_i).\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Monte Carlo integration A difficult integral becomes a sample average
once it is written as an expectation.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Example: an integral without a simple closed
form}\label{example-an-integral-without-a-simple-closed-form}

Consider \[I=\int_0^1 e^{-x^3}\,\,dx.\] Let
\(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Since the density of \(U\) is
\(1\) on \([0,1]\), \[I=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-U^3}\right].\] Generate
\(U_1,\ldots,U_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\)
and define \[W_i=e^{-U_i^3}.\] Then
\[\widehat{I}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-U_i^3}\] estimates \(I\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 8} (Monte Carlo integration). Design a Monte Carlo
estimator for \[\int_0^1 e^{-x^3}\,\,dx.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let
\(U_1,\ldots,U_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).
Use \[\widehat{I}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N e^{-U_i^3}.\] By the Law of
Large Numbers, \[\widehat{I}_N \xrightarrow{P} \mathbb{E}[e^{-U^3}]
=\int_0^1 e^{-x^3}\,\,dx.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{General Monte Carlo
integration}\label{general-monte-carlo-integration}

More generally, suppose \[I=\int f(x)p(x)\,\,dx,\] where \(p(x)\) is a
probability density. If \(X_i\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}p\), then
\[\widehat{I}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(X_i)\] is the basic Monte
Carlo estimator.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 9}. When we change the sampling distribution \(p\), the
function being averaged changes. This observation leads directly to
importance sampling.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 10} (Uniform Monte Carlo integration). Use
Monte Carlo to estimate \[\int_a^b g(x)\,\,dx.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)\). Then \(p(x)=1/(b-a)\) on
\([a,b]\), and \[\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_a^b g(x)\frac{1}{b-a}\,\,dx.\]
Thus \[\int_a^b g(x)\,\,dx = (b-a)\mathbb{E}[g(X)].\] Generate
\(X_1,\ldots,X_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)\)
and use \[\widehat{I}_N=(b-a)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g(X_i).\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 11} (Practice integral). Use the Monte Carlo
method to estimate \[I=\int_{-1}^{2} \cos^2(x)(x^3+1)\,\,dx.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(-1,2)\). Then \(b-a=3\), and
\[I=3\mathbb{E}\left[\cos^2(X)(X^3+1)\right].\] Generate
\(X_1,\ldots,X_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(-1,2)\)
and compute
\[\widehat{I}_N=\frac{3}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \cos^2(X_i)(X_i^3+1).\] For
comparison, a symbolic calculation gives
\[I=\frac{3\sin 4}{2}+\frac{21\cos 4}{16}-\frac{3\cos 2}{16}+\frac{3\sin 2}{8}+\frac{27}{8}
\approx 1.8009.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 12} (Practice integral). Use Monte Carlo to
estimate \[I=\int_0^1 \frac{e^x-1}{e-1}\,\,dx.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Then
\[I=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{e^U-1}{e-1}\right].\] The Monte Carlo
estimator is
\[\widehat{I}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{e^{U_i}-1}{e-1},
\qquad U_i\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).\] The
exact value is \[I=\frac{1}{e-1}\int_0^1(e^x-1)\,\,dx
=\frac{e-2}{e-1}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Application III: Bayesian Inference and
Learning}\label{application-iii-bayesian-inference-and-learning}

This section shows why Monte Carlo methods are central in Bayesian
statistics.

Let \(X\in\mathcal{X}\) be an unknown variable and let \(Y\) be observed
data. Bayesian inference often requires integrals that are analytically
intractable.

\section{Normalization}\label{normalization}

Bayes' theorem gives \[p(X\mid Y)=\frac{p(Y\mid X)p(X)}{p(Y)}.\] The
normalizing constant is
\[p(Y)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(Y\mid X')p(X')\,\,dX'.\] This integral may be
difficult in high dimensions.

If \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(S)}\) are sampled from the prior \(p(X)\), then
\[p(Y)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p(X)}[p(Y\mid X)]
\approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S p(Y\mid x^{(s)}).\]

\section{Marginalization}\label{marginalization-1}

If a model contains latent variables \(Z\), the marginal posterior may
require \[p(X\mid Y)=\int p(X,Z\mid Y)\,\,dZ.\] Monte Carlo methods
approximate this integral using samples from a suitable distribution.

\section{Posterior expectations}\label{posterior-expectations}

Many Bayesian summaries are posterior expectations:
\[\mathbb{E}_{p(X\mid Y)}[f(X)]
=\int_{\mathcal{X}} f(X)p(X\mid Y)\,\,dX.\] If
\(X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(S)}\) are samples from \(p(X\mid Y)\), then
\[\mathbb{E}_{p(X\mid Y)}[f(X)]\approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S f(X^{(s)}).\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 13}. In Bayesian inference, Monte Carlo is often needed
because the posterior distribution is known only up to a normalizing
constant.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Application IV:
Optimization}\label{application-iv-optimization}

This section shows how random sampling can be used to search for good
solutions of optimization problems.

\section{Random search}\label{random-search}

Optimization problems ask us to minimize or maximize an objective
function, often in many dimensions. Random search is a simple Monte
Carlo optimization method.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ objective\_function(x):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ x}\OperatorTok{**}\DecValTok{2}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ random\_search(objective\_function, bounds, max\_iter}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    best\_solution }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{None}
\NormalTok{    best\_score }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}inf\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(max\_iter):}
\NormalTok{        solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.uniform(bounds[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], bounds[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{        score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ objective\_function(solution)}

        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ score }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ best\_score:}
\NormalTok{            best\_solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ solution}
\NormalTok{            best\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ score}

    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ best\_solution, best\_score}

\NormalTok{bounds }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{best\_solution, best\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ random\_search(objective\_function, bounds)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Best solution:"}\NormalTok{, best\_solution)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Best score:"}\NormalTok{, best\_score)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 14} (Random search). Explain why random search can be
useful even though it seems inefficient.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Random search does not follow a deterministic gradient direction.
Instead, it samples many candidate points from the search space. This
can be useful when the objective function is non-convex, discontinuous,
noisy, or has many local minima. It is also easy to implement and can
work surprisingly well in high-dimensional hyperparameter search when
only a small number of dimensions are truly important.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Simulated annealing}\label{simulated-annealing}

Simulated annealing is a Monte Carlo method for global optimization. It
is designed for complicated, multimodal, or non-convex objective
functions.

The method proposes random neighboring states. A better state is
accepted automatically, while a worse state may still be accepted with
probability depending on a temperature parameter. The temperature is
gradually decreased.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ objective\_function(x):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.sin(x) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.sin(}\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{x)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ simulated\_annealing(objective\_function, bounds,}
\NormalTok{                        initial\_temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{                        cooling\_rate}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{                        num\_iterations}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    current\_solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.uniform(bounds[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], bounds[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{    current\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ objective\_function(current\_solution)}
\NormalTok{    best\_solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ current\_solution}
\NormalTok{    best\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ current\_score}
\NormalTok{    temperature }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ initial\_temperature}
\NormalTok{    solution\_history }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [(current\_solution, current\_score)]}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(num\_iterations):}
\NormalTok{        neighbor\_solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ current\_solution }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.random.uniform(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        neighbor\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ objective\_function(neighbor\_solution)}

        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ (neighbor\_score }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ current\_score }\KeywordTok{or}
\NormalTok{            np.random.rand() }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ np.exp((current\_score }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ neighbor\_score) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ temperature)):}
\NormalTok{            current\_solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ neighbor\_solution}
\NormalTok{            current\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ neighbor\_score}

        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ current\_score }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ best\_score:}
\NormalTok{            best\_solution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ current\_solution}
\NormalTok{            best\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ current\_score}

\NormalTok{        temperature }\OperatorTok{*=}\NormalTok{ cooling\_rate}
\NormalTok{        solution\_history.append((current\_solution, current\_score))}

    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ best\_solution, best\_score, solution\_history}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Common Distributions Used in Monte
Carlo}\label{common-distributions-used-in-monte-carlo}

This section reviews probability distributions frequently used in Monte
Carlo modeling.

Common probability distributions include:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Uniform distribution:} models equally likely values over an
  interval.
\item
  \textbf{Normal distribution:} models symmetric noise and appears
  naturally through the Central Limit Theorem.
\item
  \textbf{Exponential distribution:} models waiting times between
  independent events.
\item
  \textbf{Poisson distribution:} models event counts over time or space.
\item
  \textbf{Discrete distributions:} model categorical outcomes or finite
  sample spaces.
\item
  \textbf{Lognormal distribution:} models positive variables whose
  logarithm is normal.
\item
  \textbf{Triangular distribution:} a continuous distribution on
  \([a,b]\) with mode \(c\), where \(a<b\) and \(a\le c\le b\).
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 15} (Triangular distribution). A triangular
distribution with lower limit \(a\), upper limit \(b\), and mode \(c\)
has density \[f(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2(x-a)}{(b-a)(c-a)}, & a\le x\le c,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{2(b-x)}{(b-a)(b-c)}, & c<x\le b,\\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Random Number Generation}\label{random-number-generation}

This section discusses the starting point of Monte Carlo: generating
random numbers.

\section{Uniform random variables}\label{uniform-random-variables}

Most random number generation begins with samples from a uniform
distribution on \([0,1]\). The general workflow is:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Generate IID uniform random numbers
  \(U_1,U_2,\ldots\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).
\item
  Transform those uniform random numbers into samples from another
  desired distribution.
\end{enumerate}

If a target density \(f\) has CDF \[F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,\,dt,\]
then the inverse-transform method uses \(F^{-1}\) to transform uniform
draws into samples from \(F\).

\section{Pseudorandom number
generators}\label{pseudorandom-number-generators}

In practice, computers generate pseudorandom numbers. A basic example is
a linear congruential generator.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 16} (Linear congruential generator). Choose a
starting seed \(X_0\) and constants \(a,c,m\). Generate
\[X_{n+1}=(aX_n+c)\mod m.\] Then \[U_n=\frac{X_n}{m}\] can be treated as
an approximate uniform number in \([0,1]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 17}. The mathematical details of pseudorandom number
generation are outside the scope of this course, but the quality of the
random number generator can affect Monte Carlo accuracy.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Standard Distributions: Inverse-Transform
Method}\label{standard-distributions-inverse-transform-method}

This section develops the inverse-transform method for sampling from
nonuniform distributions.

\section{General inverse-transform
method}\label{general-inverse-transform-method}

Suppose \(Z\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and suppose the target
random variable \(Y\) has CDF \(h(y)\). Define \[Y=h^{-1}(Z).\] Then
\(Y\) has CDF \(h\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 18} (Inverse-transform sampling). \emph{Let
\(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and let \(F\) be a continuous,
strictly increasing CDF. Define \[Y=F^{-1}(U).\] Then \(Y\) has CDF
\(F\).}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For any \(y\), \[\mathbb{P}(Y\le y)=\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U)\le y).\] Since
\(F\) is increasing, this event is equivalent to \(U\le F(y)\).
Therefore, \[\mathbb{P}(Y\le y)=\mathbb{P}(U\le F(y))=F(y),\] because
\(U\) is uniform on \([0,1]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Example: exponential
distribution}\label{example-exponential-distribution}

Let \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) with density
\[p(y)=\lambda e^{-\lambda y},\qquad y\ge 0.\] Its CDF is
\[h(y)=1-e^{-\lambda y}.\] Set \(z=h(y)\). Then \[z=1-e^{-\lambda y}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1-z=e^{-\lambda y}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 y=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\log(1-z).\] Thus, if
\(Z\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), then
\[Y=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\log(1-Z)\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda).\] Since
\(1-Z\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), one often writes
\[Y=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\log U.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 19} (Exponential inverse transform). Generate samples
from \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) using uniform random variables.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Since \(\lambda=2\),
\[Y=-\frac{1}{2}\log(1-U)\] has the exponential distribution with rate
\(2\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Example: Cauchy
distribution}\label{example-cauchy-distribution}

The Cauchy distribution with location \(x_0\) and scale \(\gamma\) has
density
\[p(x;x_0,\gamma)=\frac{1}{\pi\gamma}\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\gamma}\right)^2}.\]
Its CDF is
\[F(x;x_0,\gamma)=\frac{1}{\pi}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\gamma}\right)+\frac{1}{2}.\]
Solving \(z=F(x)\) gives the inverse CDF
\[x=F^{-1}(z)=x_0+\gamma\tan\left(\pi\left(z-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right).\]
Therefore, if \(Z\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), then
\[X=x_0+\gamma\tan\left(\pi\left(Z-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)\] follows a
\(\operatorname{Cauchy}(x_0,\gamma)\) distribution.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 20} (Cauchy inverse transform). Generate samples from
the standard Cauchy distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For the standard Cauchy distribution, \(x_0=0\) and \(\gamma=1\). If
\(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), then
\[X=\tan\left(\pi\left(U-\frac12\right)\right)\] has the standard Cauchy
distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}

\chapter{Multiple Variables and the Box--Muller
Method}\label{multiple-variables-and-the-boxmuller-method}

This section extends random variable transformations to multiple
variables.

\section{Jacobian transformation}\label{jacobian-transformation}

Suppose \(u_1,
\ldots,u_M\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) and we define a
transformation from \(u\) variables to \(y\) variables. The density
transformation is controlled by the Jacobian:
\[p(y_1,\ldots,y_M)=p(u_1,\ldots,u_M)
\left|\frac{\partial(u_1,\ldots,u_M)}{\partial(y_1,\ldots,y_M)}\right|.\]

\section{Polar transformation of two normal
variables}\label{polar-transformation-of-two-normal-variables}

Let \(Z_1,Z_2\) be independent standard normal variables. Their joint
density is
\[f(z_1,z_2)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\exp\left(-\frac{z_1^2+z_2^2}{2}\right).\]
Transform to polar coordinates: \[Z_1=R\cos\Theta,
\qquad
Z_2=R\sin\Theta.\] Since \(R^2=Z_1^2+Z_2^2\) and the Jacobian is \(R\),
the joint density of \((R,\Theta)\) is
\[f_{R,\Theta}(r,\theta)=\frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2}r,
\qquad r>0,\\ 0\le \theta<2\pi.\] Therefore,
\[\Theta\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,2\pi),\] and
\[f_R(r)=re^{-r^2/2},\qquad r>0.\] The CDF of \(R\) is
\[F_R(r)=1-e^{-r^2/2}.\] Thus, if
\(U_1,U_2\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\),
\[R=\sqrt{-2\log U_1},
\qquad
\Theta=2\pi U_2.\]

\section{Box--Muller method}\label{boxmuller-method}

The Box--Muller method converts two independent uniform random variables
into two independent standard normal random variables.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Theorem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Theorem 21} (Box--Muller method). \emph{Let
\(U_1,U_2\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Define
\[Z_1=\sqrt{-2\log U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2),\]
\[Z_2=\sqrt{-2\log U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2).\] Then \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) are
independent standard normal random variables.}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The construction uses polar coordinates. The angle \(\Theta=2\pi U_2\)
is uniform on \([0,2\pi]\). The radius \(R=\sqrt{-2\log U_1}\) has CDF
\[\mathbb{P}(R\le r)=\mathbb{P}\left(\sqrt{-2\log U_1}\le r\right)
=\mathbb{P}(U_1\ge e^{-r^2/2})=1-e^{-r^2/2}.\] This is exactly the
Rayleigh distribution needed for the radius of a two-dimensional
standard normal vector. Therefore \((Z_1,Z_2)\) has joint density
\[\frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-(z_1^2+z_2^2)/2},\] which factors into two standard
normal densities.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Rejection Sampling}\label{rejection-sampling}

This section introduces rejection sampling, a method for sampling from a
complex target distribution using a simpler proposal distribution.

\section{Setup}\label{setup}

Suppose we want to sample from a target density \(p(z)\), but direct
sampling is difficult. Choose a proposal density \(q(z)\) from which it
is easy to sample. Assume there exists a constant \(k<\infty\) such that
\[p(z)\le kq(z)
\qquad\text{for all }z.\] The function \(kq(z)\) forms an envelope above
\(p(z)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 22} (Proposal distribution). In rejection sampling,
\(q(z)\) is called the proposal distribution because it proposes
candidate samples.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Algorithm}\label{algorithm}

~

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Rejection sampling algorithm Repeat the following steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Sample \(Z\sim q(z)\).
\item
  Sample \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) independently.
\item
  Accept \(Z\) if \[U\le \frac{p(Z)}{kq(Z)}.\] Otherwise reject \(Z\)
  and try again.
\end{enumerate}

The accepted samples have density \(p(z)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 23} (Acceptance probability). Show that the overall
probability of acceptance is \(1/k\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Conditioning on the proposed value \(Z=z\),
\[\mathbb{P}(\text{accept}\mid Z=z)=\frac{p(z)}{kq(z)}.\] Therefore
\[\mathbb{P}(\text{accept})
=\int \mathbb{P}(\text{accept}\mid Z=z)q(z)\,\,dz
=\int \frac{p(z)}{kq(z)}q(z)\,\,dz
=\frac{1}{k}\int p(z)\,\,dz
=\frac{1}{k}.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Limitations}\label{limitations}

Rejection sampling is simple and exact in principle, but it may be
inefficient.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  It may be hard to find a finite and useful \(k\) such that
  \(p(z)\le kq(z)\) everywhere.
\item
  If \(k\) is too large, the acceptance probability \(1/k\) is too
  small.
\item
  In high-dimensional spaces, most proposed points may be rejected,
  making the method exponentially slow.
\end{itemize}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Importance Sampling}\label{importance-sampling}

This section introduces importance sampling, a method for estimating
expectations by sampling from a convenient proposal distribution.

\section{Basic importance sampling
identity}\label{basic-importance-sampling-identity}

Suppose we want \[\mathbb{E}_p[f(Z)] = \int f(z)p(z)\,\,dz,\] but
sampling from \(p\) is difficult. Choose a proposal density \(q\) such
that \(q(z)>0\) whenever \(p(z)f(z)\ne 0\). Then \[\mathbb{E}_p[f(Z)]
=\int f(z)\frac{p(z)}{q(z)}q(z)\,\,dz.\] If
\(Z^{(1)},\ldots,Z^{(L)}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}q\), then
\[\widehat{I}_L
=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^L
\frac{p(Z^{(\ell)})}{q(Z^{(\ell)})}f(Z^{(\ell)})\] estimates
\(\mathbb{E}_p[f(Z)]\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 24} (Importance weights). The ratios
\[r_\ell=\frac{p(Z^{(\ell)})}{q(Z^{(\ell)})}\] are called importance
weights. They correct the bias introduced by sampling from \(q\) instead
of \(p\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 25}. Unlike rejection sampling, importance sampling keeps
all generated samples. However, the estimator can have high variance if
the weights are unstable.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Self-normalized importance
sampling}\label{self-normalized-importance-sampling}

Often, especially in Bayesian statistics, the target density is known
only up to a normalizing constant:
\[p(z)=\frac{\widetilde{p}(z)}{Z_p}.\] Similarly, we may write
\[q(z)=\frac{\widetilde{q}(z)}{Z_q}.\] Then \[\mathbb{E}_p[f]
=\frac{Z_q}{Z_p}\int f(z)\frac{\widetilde{p}(z)}{\widetilde{q}(z)}q(z)\,\,dz.\]
The ratio of normalizing constants can be estimated by \[\frac{Z_p}{Z_q}
=\int \frac{\widetilde{p}(z)}{\widetilde{q}(z)}q(z)\,\,dz
\approx \frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^L \widetilde{r}_\ell,\] where
\[\widetilde{r}_\ell=\frac{\widetilde{p}(Z^{(\ell)})}{\widetilde{q}(Z^{(\ell)})}.\]
Thus the self-normalized estimator is \[\widehat{I}_{SN}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell f(Z^{(\ell)}),\] where
\[w_\ell=\frac{\widetilde{r}_\ell}{\sum_{m=1}^L \widetilde{r}_m}
=\frac{\widetilde{p}(Z^{(\ell)})/\widetilde{q}(Z^{(\ell)})}{\sum_{m=1}^L \widetilde{p}(Z^{(m)})/\widetilde{q}(Z^{(m)})}.\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 26} (Importance sampling for rare events). Suppose \(p\)
puts very small probability in a region that contributes a lot to the
expectation. Explain why a proposal \(q\) can help.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

If direct samples from \(p\) rarely visit the important region, the
ordinary Monte Carlo average will have high variance. A proposal \(q\)
can intentionally sample more often from the important region. The
weight \(p(z)/q(z)\) then corrects the estimator so it still targets the
original expectation under \(p\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Sampling-Importance-Resampling}\label{sampling-importance-resampling}

This section explains how importance weights can be used to
approximately draw samples from a target distribution.

Rejection sampling requires a constant \(k\) satisfying
\(p(z)\le kq(z)\), which may be hard to find.
Sampling-importance-resampling avoids this envelope constant.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Sampling-importance-resampling (SIR)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Draw proposal samples \(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(L)}\sim q(z)\).
\item
  Compute weights \[w_\ell\propto \frac{p(z^{(\ell)})}{q(z^{(\ell)})},
  \qquad \sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell=1.\]
\item
  Resample from the discrete set \(\{z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(L)}\}\) with
  probabilities \(w_1,\ldots,w_L\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

The second-stage resampled values are approximate samples from the
target distribution \(p\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Remark}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\emph{Remark 27}. SIR is conceptually useful because it transforms
weighted samples into unweighted samples, but it can suffer from weight
degeneracy if a small number of weights dominate.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Summary, Advantages, and
Limitations}\label{summary-advantages-and-limitations}

This section summarizes the main Monte Carlo methods and their practical
strengths and weaknesses.

\section{Summary of methods}\label{summary-of-methods}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Main idea} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Monte Carlo simulation & Approximate probabilities or expectations by
repeated random experiments. \\
Monte Carlo integration & Rewrite an integral as an expectation and
approximate it by a sample average. \\
Inverse-transform sampling & Generate samples by applying an inverse CDF
to uniform random variables. \\
Box--Muller method & Generate two independent normal random variables
from two independent uniforms. \\
Rejection sampling & Sample from a proposal and accept/reject candidates
to obtain target samples. \\
Importance sampling & Sample from a proposal and correct using
weights. \\
Sampling-importance-resampling & Use importance weights to resample
approximate draws from the target. \\
\end{longtable}
}

\section{Advantages}\label{advantages}

Monte Carlo methods are widely used because they are often easy to
implement and broadly applicable.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  They can solve complex problems using simple random sampling.
\item
  They turn difficult integrals into averages.
\item
  Randomness becomes a tool rather than an obstacle.
\item
  They scale conceptually to high-dimensional statistical models.
\end{itemize}

\section{Limitations}\label{limitations-1}

Monte Carlo methods also have important limitations.

\begin{itemize}
\item
  They may require substantial computational power.
\item
  Accuracy depends on the number of samples and the variance of the
  estimator.
\item
  Results can be sensitive to the chosen sampling distribution.
\item
  Basic Monte Carlo can perform poorly for high-dimensional integration
  or rare-event problems.
\item
  Rejection sampling may be inefficient when acceptance rates are small.
\item
  Importance sampling may be unstable when weights have high variance.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Warning}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Alan Sokal's warning ``Monte Carlo is an extremely bad method; it should
be used only when all alternative methods are worse.''

This quote emphasizes that Monte Carlo is powerful, but not magic. It is
most useful when exact calculation, deterministic integration, or direct
optimization is impractical.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Additional Practice
Problems}\label{additional-practice-problems-2}

This section gives additional exercises to reinforce the main ideas of
Monte Carlo sampling.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 28} (Variance of the Monte Carlo estimator).
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_N\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}p\) and define
\[\widehat{I}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(X_i).\] Assume
\(\operatorname{Var}(f(X))<\infty\). Find \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I}_N]\)
and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{I}_N)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By linearity of expectation,
\[\mathbb{E}[\widehat{I}_N]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}[f(X_i)]=\mathbb{E}[f(X)].\]
Thus the estimator is unbiased for \(I=\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\).

Because the samples are independent,
\[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{I}_N)=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N \operatorname{Var}(f(X_i))
=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f(X))}{N}.\] Therefore the standard deviation
of the estimator decreases at rate \(1/\sqrt{N}\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 29} (Inverse transform for a power
distribution). Suppose \(Y\) has CDF \(F(y)=y^\alpha\) for
\(0\le y\le 1\), where \(\alpha>0\). Use inverse-transform sampling to
generate \(Y\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Solve \[U=F(y)=y^\alpha.\]
Then \[y=U^{1/\alpha}.\] Therefore \[Y=U^{1/\alpha}\] has CDF
\(F(y)=y^\alpha\) on \([0,1]\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 30} (Importance sampling identity). Let \(p\)
and \(q\) be densities with \(p(z)>0\) only where \(q(z)>0\). Show that
\[\int f(z)p(z)\,\,dz
=\mathbb{E}_q\left[f(Z)\frac{p(Z)}{q(Z)}\right].\]

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

By definition of expectation under \(q\),
\[\mathbb{E}_q\left[f(Z)\frac{p(Z)}{q(Z)}\right]
=\int f(z)\frac{p(z)}{q(z)}q(z)\,\,dz
=\int f(z)p(z)\,\,dz.\] This is the basic identity behind importance
sampling.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Practice Problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Practice Problem 31} (Acceptance rate). In rejection sampling,
suppose \(p(z)\le kq(z)\) and \(k=5\). What is the expected acceptance
probability? Approximately how many proposal samples are needed to
obtain \(1000\) accepted samples?

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The acceptance probability is
\[\mathbb{P}(\text{accept})=\frac{1}{k}=\frac{1}{5}=0.2.\] To obtain
about \(1000\) accepted samples, we need approximately
\[\frac{1000}{0.2}=5000\] proposal samples.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Chapter 11: Sufficient Statistics and the Likelihood
Principle}\label{chapter-11-sufficient-statistics-and-the-likelihood-principle}

This chapter introduces sufficient statistics as a formal data-reduction
principle for statistical inference. The main goal is to identify when a
statistic keeps all information in the sample about an unknown
parameter. The chapter also introduces the likelihood function and the
likelihood principle.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Topics}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Statistics and estimators; heuristic and mathematical definitions of
sufficient statistics; the factorization theorem; Bernoulli, normal,
uniform, and gamma examples; minimal and complete sufficient statistics;
likelihood functions; likelihood principle; binomial versus negative
binomial coin-tossing example.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Overview}\label{overview-8}

This section introduces sufficient statistics, which formalize the idea
of reducing a data set without losing information about an unknown
parameter.

In statistical inference, the data set may contain many observations,
but often the information relevant to a parameter can be summarized by a
lower-dimensional statistic. For example, for Bernoulli data, the total
number of successes contains all the information about the success
probability. For normal data with known variance, the sample mean
contains all the information about the unknown mean.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A statistic is \emph{sufficient} for a parameter if, after the statistic
is known, the remaining details of the sample no longer contain
information about the parameter.
\[\text{full data} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{sufficient statistic} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{inference about } \theta.\]

\end{tcolorbox}

The main tool in this section is the \textbf{factorization theorem}. It
gives an efficient way to check sufficiency by factoring the joint
density or joint mass function into two parts: one part involving the
parameter only through the statistic, and one part independent of the
parameter.

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Statistics and Estimators}\label{statistics-and-estimators}

This section recalls the basic language of statistics before defining
sufficient statistics.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 1} (Statistic). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random
sample from a population. A \textbf{statistic} is any function of the
sample, \[T=T(X_1,\ldots,X_n),\] that does not depend on unknown
parameters.

\end{tcolorbox}

A statistic is itself a random variable, because it is computed from
random data. After the data are observed, the statistic takes a
numerical value.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 2} (Common statistics). Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a
random sample.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  The sample mean \[\overline X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\] is a
  statistic.
\item
  The sample variance
  \[S^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\overline X)^2\] is a statistic.
\item
  The maximum \[X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}\] is a statistic.
\item
  The constant statistic \(T=3\) is also technically a statistic,
  although it ignores the data.
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Each quantity listed is a function of \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and does not
use an unknown parameter. Therefore each is a statistic. The constant
statistic is mathematically allowed, but it is usually not useful
because it does not summarize any sample information.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 3} (Estimator). A statistic \(T(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is
called an \textbf{estimator} of a population parameter \(\theta\) if it
is used to estimate \(\theta\).

\end{tcolorbox}

For example, \(\overline X\) is commonly used to estimate the population
mean \(\mu\), and \(S^2\) is commonly used to estimate the population
variance \(\sigma^2\).

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Heuristic Meaning of Sufficient
Statistics}\label{heuristic-meaning-of-sufficient-statistics}

This section explains the intuitive meaning of sufficiency before giving
the formal definition.

A sufficient statistic is a function of the data that captures all the
information needed to estimate a parameter \(\theta\). Once the
sufficient statistic is known, the rest of the data provides no
additional information about \(\theta\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Definition}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Definition 4} (Heuristic definition of sufficiency). Let
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample from a model with unknown
parameter \(\theta\). A statistic \[T=T(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\] is
\textbf{sufficient} for \(\theta\) if a statistician who knows only
\(T\) can do just as well for inference about \(\theta\) as a
statistician who knows the full data set \((X_1,\ldots,X_n)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Key idea}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Sufficiency is a data-reduction principle:
\[(X_1,\ldots,X_n) \quad \leadsto \quad T(X_1,\ldots,X_n).\] If \(T\) is
sufficient, then this reduction does not lose information about
\(\theta\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Example}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

\textbf{Example 5} (Bernoulli intuition). Suppose
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\).
Each \(X_i\) is \(1\) for success and \(0\) for failure. If the goal is
to learn \(p\), the order of successes and failures does not matter. The
total number of successes \[T=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\] contains all
information about \(p\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Solution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For example, the sequences
\[(1,1,0,1,0) \quad \text{and} \quad (0,1,1,0,1)\] both have three
successes out of five trials. Their probabilities under the Bernoulli
model are both proportional to \[p^3(1-p)^2.\] For inference about
\(p\), the relevant information is the number of successes, not the
order in which they occurred.

\end{tcolorbox}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Mathematical Definition of Sufficient
Statistics}\label{mathematical-definition-of-sufficient-statistics}

This section gives the formal conditional-distribution definition of
sufficiency.
